The 2H winner, spread and total series cannot be priced from pregame inputs alone once the market trades through halftime. TIMING: live-only (known at halftime, pregame_knowable=no); used for in-play 2H pricing and excluded from the pregame input list.
The three second-half series need an explicit pregame 2H expectation including overtime; without it they would be priced as a copy of the 1H model.

interactions.hypothesis: First-half totals depend on first-half pace, which differs from game pace and is team-specific.
A starter's early fouls create the biggest first-half-specific variance.
Half total, half spread and game lines must be coherent; inconsistent half prices are the main edge.
Late-half bonus FT scoring increases first-half totals for teams with good FT shooters.

First-half scoring equals first-half possessions times first-half points per possession; a team that starts fast (high half pace ratio) and shoots above shot quality early gets the product of both advantages, while the second half is not affected, so the effect lives only in the half contract.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress first-half points on adjusted tempo, half pace ratio, and their product while controlling for the game total; check whether the product term adds out-of-sample power.

interactions.hypothesis: A star starter's early foul trouble costs minutes only if the coach sits at two fouls, and costs more if the replacement is a much weaker unit; the net first-half impact is the product of foul probability, benching policy and the gap between starter and substitute.
interactions.how_to_test: Using historical games with a starter at two first-half fouls, compare the half margin shift by coach policy bucket and replacement gap.

interactions.hypothesis: Once a team reaches the seventh foul in the half its opponent gets one-and-one chances and at the tenth two shots, so the value of each additional foul steps up; teams with 75 percent or better free-throw shooters gain much more than poor ones, producing a threshold-by-skill interaction late in the half.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare points per possession in the last four minutes of the first half in bonus versus pre-bonus states split by team free-throw percentage tercile.

interactions.hypothesis: For 2H contracts that include overtime, the second-half margin distribution is a mixture of the regulation second half and the overtime period, and the probability of reaching overtime depends on the halftime margin and the pregame expectation together; a halftime lead of 15 nearly removes the OT component.
interactions.how_to_test: Condition historical games on halftime margin buckets and compute the share that reach overtime and the shift in 2H margin variance.

interactions.hypothesis: Because the first half has about 33 possessions, a hot or cold shooting start is a larger share of the half outcome for slow teams that have fewer possessions, so the regression weight on recent shooting luck should rise as the expected half possession count falls.
interactions.how_to_test: Test whether the sensitivity of 1H points to last-10-game 3P% deviation differs between slow-starting and fast-starting teams.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold at two first-half fouls with a coach-dependent step down in minutes
nonlinearities.why: Minutes lost are zero until the second foul and then drop by 4 to 8 minutes in the half, so the expected cost is not proportional to the foul rate; the discontinuity at the second foul produces an asymmetric variance contribution.

nonlinearities.shape: step increase in free-throw value at the 7th and 10th team fouls
nonlinearities.why: Each foul before the bonus gives a side-out, each foul after gives one or two shots; the scoring yield of the final minutes of the half therefore jumps non-linearly in team fouls, particularly for good free-throw teams.

nonlinearities.shape: peaked discrete pmf at zero decaying with expected-margin magnitude; not Gaussian near zero
nonlinearities.why: A tie needs an exact integer margin of 0 given lumps of 1 to 3 points; its probability falls from about 5.5 percent for even teams to under 3 percent when the expected half margin is above 8, a shape that a normal with equal sd mis-estimates at the centre.

mechanism_review.summary: A first-half contract reads only twenty minutes of play, about 32 to 35 possessions per team, so luck is a larger share of the outcome than in a full game: the half margin has an sd near 7 to 7.5 points against about 10 to 11 for the game, ties occur about 5 percent of the time, and a handful of three-pointers swings the total. Starters, not the bench, play most of the half (around 15 to 17 of the 20 minutes), so the opening lineup, early foul trouble (many coaches sit a player at two first-half fouls) and the coach's substitution pattern determine the real rotation. Pace in a first half differs from the whole-game pace because the second half carries bonus free throws, intentional fouling and clock management. The second-half markets, which are listed over the same game and include overtime, are conditional on the halftime state when traded live, so a halftime update term is required.

stages.name: Opening lineup and first-half rotation
stages.description: Most first-half minutes go to five starters, with the first substitution typically around the 16:00 to 12:00 mark and the bench carrying the late first half. Whether a key starter is playing and when the coach rests him in the half decides the quality of lineups on the floor. Some coaches platoon five-man units, others play starters through the half; the scheme is a coach trait. Starter lists often arrive close to tip.
stages.distribution: Discrete mixture over rotation scenarios; starters' first-half minutes are bounded in roughly 12 to 20 and positively skewed toward the maximum for stars with no foul trouble.

stages.name: Early foul trouble as a threshold event
stages.description: A player picking up two fouls in the first half is usually benched by cautious coaches for a stretch, which removes a starter exactly when the half's possessions are being decided; the probability depends on the player's foul rate per minute, the opponent's rim-attacking style and the crew's calls. This is a threshold event with a coach policy, not a smooth linear function of the foul rate.
stages.distribution: Binomial-like count of fouls with a policy-driven discrete drop in minutes; per-player probability of two or more first-half fouls ranges from about 10 to 35 percent depending on role and style.

stages.name: First-half possessions and scoring rate
stages.description: First-half possessions are fewer than half of the regulation possessions because the second half carries intentional fouling and bonus stoppages, and teams differ in how fast they start (some are early-offence teams, others walk the ball up). Points per possession in the half follow adjusted offence and defence, but three-point shooting luck over only 30 to 35 possessions is a large share of the variance and does not repeat in the second half.
stages.distribution: Half possessions approximately normal around 32 to 35 per team with sd near 2; half-level points per possession have sd about 15 percent of the mean, with strong three-point luck.

stages.name: Half-end structure and bonus dynamics
stages.description: The last four minutes of a half contain predictable structure: fouls accumulate toward the seventh team foul (one-and-one) and tenth (two shots), the leading team may hold the ball for the last shot, and a two-for-one is possible. Teams with strong free throw shooting and foul-prone defences get more value from this window. It affects the total and the spread by a few points and the same structure recurs in each half because team fouls reset at halftime; the second half adds intentional fouling by the trailing team in the last minutes and, if tied, overtime (see cbb.second_half_pregame_expectation).
stages.distribution: Late-half scoring is a regime change at the foul-count thresholds; bonus entry timing is stochastic with sd of about 2 minutes.

stages.name: Half margin and tie as a discrete distribution
stages.description: The half margin is an integer random variable with sd about 7 to 7.5 points, centred on roughly 0.55 of the game's expected margin; its pmf has a spike at zero with scoring lumps of 1, 2 and 3 points so that parity effects matter. The tie contract and the spread rungs near zero read this pmf directly, while the half total reads an approximately normal sum. The correlation between half margin and final margin is about 0.7, which makes consistency with game lines a check rather than an input. Both three-way listings (KXNCAAMB1H and KXNCAAMB1HWINNER) read the zero-margin spike as their Tie strike.
stages.distribution: Discrete pmf, near-normal with a central spike; tie probability about 5 percent and a tie-aware spread ladder; second-half margin distribution is wider because of OT and late fouling.

stages.name: Halftime state update for second-half markets
stages.description: Once the first half is over, 2H markets depend on the halftime score and on events in the first half: foul counts of key players, who is in foul trouble, shooting that was far above or below shot quality, and the lead's effect on coaching (lead protection, tempo slowdown). The second-half margin is only weakly related to the halftime margin once strength is known, but the first-half evidence is informative about strength and availability. A pregame-only model cannot price these markets live. For pregame pricing of the 2H series the explicit input cbb.second_half_pregame_expectation (regulation expectation minus the 1H expectation plus late-foul and overtime terms) is used; cbb.halftime_state_adjustment is live-only (known at halftime) and is excluded from the pregame feature set. The overtime, blowout and late-foul terms here use the fundamentals expected margin; the catalog versions bucketed by closing spread are benchmarks only.
stages.distribution: Conditional distribution: second-half margin has mean pulled toward the pregame expectation (not the halftime lead) with a small slowdown of pace when ahead; additional variance from overtime (5 to 6 percent of games).

talent_strength.note: Opponent-adjusted efficiency drives first-half scoring; the team-specific half split is mostly noise and needs heavy shrinkage.

opponent_matchup.note: No attached input captures how the opponent's first-half scheme (early foul-drawing, press pressure at the start) changes the half, and no free source gives half-level scheme splits.

role_personnel.note: Starters play most of the half, so who starts and how many minutes they play is first order.

availability_news.note: Opening lineup is announced close to tip; a missing starter has a larger share of effect in a half dominated by starters.

coaching_scheme.note: Substitution timing and the two-foul benching rule are coach policies that drive the first-half rotation.

environment.note: Venue and crowd effects act mostly on the full-game margin and on late-game free throws; no attached or known first-half-specific environment variable is distinguishable from the margin-wide home edge over a 20-minute half.

game_context_script.note: Half-end foul structure and halftime-conditional script are explicit; blowout is relevant to the 2H markets only. Pregame 2H series: regulation expectation minus 1H plus late-foul and overtime terms (cbb.second_half_pregame_expectation); halftime_state_adjustment is live-only.

pace_volume.note: First-half possessions differ from half of the game tempo; the ratio is team-specific.

efficiency_conversion.note: Three-point shooting over 30 to 35 possessions drives a large share of half variance.

distribution_variance.note: Integer pmf with a central spike for the tie contract.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest, travel and rivalry effects change a team's average effort and fatigue across the game and cannot be separated from noise in a 20-minute half sample of 15 to 30 games per team.

officiating_rules.note: Crew whistle tendency feeds early foul trouble and the bonus timing; crews are usually unknown until game day.

settlement_contract.note: Half-only points, tie as a separate contract, OT included only in the 2H series.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Seven half-level series on one game. KXNCAAMB1H and KXNCAAMB1HWINNER are first-half winner markets with a separate Tie outcome (1HWINNER: 'first half of regulation time'; if both teams score the same, all team strikes resolve No and the Tie strike Yes). KXNCAAMB1HSPREAD and KXNCAAMB1HTOTAL are .5 strikes on the first-half margin and combined first-half points. KXNCAAMB2H, 2HSPREAD and 2HTOTAL read only second-half points and explicitly include overtime. Only points scored in the named half count. Only KXNCAAMB1HWINNER carries a postponement clause (stays open for a rescheduled game within two weeks).
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Official game score by period (half), as published for the game; the rules name only 'points scored during the 1st half' so provider hierarchy for the period split is unverified.
variants_and_edge_cases: The 1H winner market has a TIE contract (YES if neither team leads at the half): probability is the integer pmf of the half margin at zero, about 4 to 6 percent for a 20-minute half, a discrete mass a normal approximation handles poorly.
2nd-half series include overtime, so the 2H margin and total contain a five-minute mixture component in the roughly 5 to 6 percent of games that go to extra time; 1st-half series never do.

Postponement: only KXNCAAMB1HWINNER states a rule (market stays open for a game rescheduled within two weeks); the 1H, 1H spread, 1H total and 2H series carry only the half-points note, so delay and cancellation handling for them is CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS.

Strikes in the sample (1H total 89.5 and 2H total 87.5) are far above a typical combined 20-minute half of about 65 to 72 points, so the live ladders include extreme tail rungs; the sample strike is not an estimate of the median.
Second-half markets are live through the first half: their information set includes the halftime score, foul counts and shooting luck, none of which exists pregame.
KXNCAAMB1H and KXNCAAMB1HWINNER are two listings of the same three-way first-half result with different templates; both price the same integer half-margin pmf.

player_props.target: A player's single-game stat over a threshold (DNP rule in rules text)
player_props.mechanism: Count = minutes x per-minute rate with overdispersion from foul trouble, blowouts, tempo and teammate availability. CBB features short rotations, roster churn and small samples (about 30 games), so parameter uncertainty and shrinkage are central; disclosure of availability is sparse, and box-score sources can be late or erroneous for smaller programs.

interactions.hypothesis: Stars on heavy favorites lose minutes in blowouts, depressing high-rung overs.
Short rotations make absences redistribute heavily; role-level priors prevent overfitting.
Small-sample hot streaks inflate averages; hierarchical shrinkage improves calibration.
Stat-provider and DNP rules combine to determine whether a marginal outcome settles on a questionable record.

When a starter is out, remaining starters absorb the minutes only if the rotation is short; in a deep rotation the freed minutes go to bench players, so the stat redistribution to any given teammate is conditional on the rotation's depth and on whether the missing player was a ball handler or a big.
interactions.how_to_test: Using games with a missing starter, regress teammate minute and stat change on the missing player's minutes share interacted with a bench-depth index (minutes of players 6 to 9).

interactions.hypothesis: The correct dispersion of a player's stat depends on how many role-stable games underlie the estimate: with few such games the posterior uncertainty adds to the sampling variance, widening the distribution and moving probability mass to both tails of the ladder.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare calibration of rung probabilities from a fixed-dispersion model against one with n_eff-dependent dispersion, stratified by n_eff terciles.

interactions.hypothesis: A shortfall in minutes lowers every stat at once, so unconditional correlations between points, rebounds and assists are mostly due to minutes; after conditioning the residual correlation is small or even negative (points and assists compete for the same possessions for a guard), so joint props need the shared minutes draw plus a residual copula.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed joint frequencies of two-stat thresholds with simulated joints from independent-given-minutes versus copula-with-residual models.

interactions.hypothesis: A scorekeeper's generosity matters only for judgement-based stats, so it adds to assists for ball handlers and blocks for rim protectors but leaves points untouched; the role selects which adjustment applies, and it matters more at small-conference venues than at power-conference ones with professional statisticians.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate home minus away assist-rate gap by role and by conference tier and check that it differs from zero only for ball handlers and non-power venues.

interactions.hypothesis: A starter's minutes fall once the expected game margin exceeds the coach's blowout trigger (a lead of 20 with eight to ten minutes left); the drop applies to every stat, and its depth is larger for scorers who sit than for rebounders who may be left in longer, so each stat has its own threshold response.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare minutes and stat per 36 by expected-margin bucket for starters on favourites and underdogs; look for a break near 15 expected points.

nonlinearities.shape: variance-to-mean ratio varies with the mean and minutes; zero inflation increases for players with fewer than 15 minutes
nonlinearities.why: Counts for low-minute players are close to a degenerate distribution near zero while those of stars are approximately Poisson-plus-overdispersion, so a single dispersion parameter distorts both the tails and the probability of exceeding 0.5 for bench players.

nonlinearities.shape: non-monotone mapping of status label to play probability with a mass near 0.5 for 'questionable' and near 0.95 for undisclosed
nonlinearities.why: A label of questionable is about as likely to mean out as in, whereas silence usually means he plays; the mapping from label to probability is a step function that depends on program and time to tip, not a smooth severity scale.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold at about 15 minutes below which counts collapse; approximately linear above
nonlinearities.why: A player who is limited to under 15 minutes produces few counting stats, while above that threshold output scales near-proportionally to minutes, so the distribution has a kink and a spike at low minutes.

mechanism_review.summary: Any counting prop is a latent player state multiplied through a common chain: does the player appear, how many minutes and in what role, how many opportunities per minute for the particular stat, and how many of those convert, with the box score as a measured (not true) record. The shared layer is what makes the generic archetype different from any single stat: availability and minutes are common to every stat, role (ball handler, wing, big) selects which stats have large rates, and the stats are correlated through minutes and game script, so combination props and parlays need a joint distribution. College adds three specific difficulties: samples of about 30 games with partial role changes, transfer-portal players with no history at the new team, and box-score statistics recorded by a home scorekeeper with variable quality.

stages.name: Appearance and the cause of non-appearance
stages.description: A prop is only meaningful if the player plays, and the probability of playing depends on why a player might not: a confirmed injury differs from an unannounced coach's decision or an eligibility ruling, and each has a different pregame signal and a different time at which the information appears. College disclosure is voluntary, so many non-appearances are surprises. The settlement rule (void or NO) decides whether this stage affects the label or only the information set.
stages.distribution: Point mass at zero for DNP (a few percent for starters, much higher for rotation players) plus a restricted-minutes component after injury.

stages.name: Role and minutes as a latent state
stages.description: Role (starter guard, wing, stretch big, rim runner) determines both the minutes envelope and which stats have large per-minute rates. Minutes depend on the rotation size, foul trouble and the probability of a blowout, and they are common to every statistic of the same player, so a minute shortfall hits points, rebounds and assists together. A shorter rotation concentrates minutes in the starters and reduces variance for them.
stages.distribution: Minutes distribution is truncated at 40 (plus overtime) with a heavy left tail from foul trouble and blowouts; position and role shift the mean by up to 10 minutes.

stages.name: Per-minute rates with hierarchical shrinkage and cold starts
stages.description: Per-minute counting rates are estimated from 30 or fewer games, with role changes between seasons and for transfers, so the estimate is a hierarchical posterior combining the player's own record, the role's prior and, for newcomers, the prior-team production translated through team quality and position. Teammate absences shift rates for the remaining players, and the effective sample size is smaller than the games played count because the role has changed.
stages.distribution: Rates have between-game overdispersion; posterior sd of the true rate is about 15 to 25 percent of the mean for players with fewer than 15 games in the current role.

stages.name: Opponent, pace and joint dependence between stats
stages.description: Opponent style changes the opportunity supply (opponent three-point volume, rebound opportunities, turnover pressure), and game pace scales every stat. The stats of one player are correlated: rebounds and points covary through minutes and in a fast game all counts rise. Combination markets and any parlay of two props from the same player need the joint distribution, which is not the product of marginals.
stages.distribution: Positive correlation between stats through shared minutes and pace (around 0.3 to 0.5 for points with rebounds in raw counts, falling after conditioning on minutes); the dependence is non-Gaussian in the tails.

stages.name: Measurement: how the box score records the stat
stages.description: The settled value is a recorded statistic, not the underlying count. Assists, steals, blocks and sometimes rebounds depend on the statistician's judgement; a home-court scorekeeper effect has been documented in professional basketball and plausibly exists in college, where scorers are volunteers or students at smaller venues. Late corrections change values after the fact.
stages.distribution: Small measurement noise with possible venue-specific bias (up to a few percent of the mean for assists and blocks), concentrated in non-power-conference venues.

stages.name: Distribution form and ladder mapping
stages.description: Counting stats are discrete with different shapes: points are overdispersed, rebounds and assists closer to Poisson with zero inflation for low-minute players, threes made are a thinned Poisson (attempts times make probability). A ladder reads the cumulative tail, so the dispersion and the zero mass matter more than the mean for extreme rungs. Overtime adds a small mixture.
stages.distribution: Negative-binomial or zero-inflated forms with stat-specific dispersion; cumulative probabilities across rungs are monotone and must be consistent with the minutes mixture.

talent_strength.note: Per-minute rates with shrinkage and a cold-start prior for transfers.

opponent_matchup.note: Opponent opportunity supply by role; small samples, so priors are important.

role_personnel.note: Role selects the stats and sets the effective sample for shrinkage.

availability_news.note: Participation split by cause; disclosure is voluntary in college.

coaching_scheme.note: Rotation size and foul-benching rules are coach choices; direct coach-level tendencies are inferred from past minutes only.

environment.note: Arena and weather conditions act on team-level pace and home advantage, which enter through tempo; no environmental variable acts on a single player's stat line beyond them in the known data.

game_context_script.note: Blowout and close-game states truncate or extend the minutes of the same player for all stats.

efficiency_conversion.note: Conversion regression for shooting stats; non-shooting stats rely on rate shrinkage.

distribution_variance.note: Marginal shapes and cross-stat dependence for combination markets.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: A single game's rest and travel effect on one player's counting stats is smaller than the sampling noise of 30 games and no stable player-level effect is known; rotation changes from schedule are captured by roster minutes.

officiating_rules.note: The crew affects fouls and thereby minutes; official scorers affect recorded assists and blocks.

settlement_contract.note: No live series and no rules text exist for generic college player props, so DNP handling, OT, source of truth and rung construction are undefined; the archetype cannot be evaluated against a contract.

contract_review.settlement_definition: No live Kalshi series exists in the ledger for this generic archetype, so there is no rules text to verify. The intended contract is a single named player's counting statistic (points, rebounds, assists, threes, or a combination) over a half-point or integer threshold in one game, settling on the official box score. What a player who does not play does to the market (void, NO, or YES for an 'under' side), whether overtime counts, how combination stats are summed, and which box-score provider is the source of truth are all unspecified and must not be inferred from the other CBB series.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Not defined (no rules text). Candidates are the official NCAA statistician's box score, ESPN, or Sports-Reference; discrepancies between them for assists and rebounds are known to exist, with a typical difference of one unit for a few percent of players.
variants_and_edge_cases: Combination props (points plus rebounds plus assists, double-double) multiply the number of stats that must settle correctly and make the provider choice and the correlation between stats first order.
Rung construction can be over/under a .5 line or an 'N or more' ladder; for a discrete count the two have identical probabilities only if the strike set is the same integer.

A player who is on the roster but does not play (injury, coach's decision, suspension, eligibility) is a DNP whose label is undefined; a player who plays three minutes is a technical appearance with almost no counting stats.
Stat corrections: college box scores for smaller venues can be edited after the game (assist credited, rebound reassigned), so the first published value may differ from the settled one.

player_points.mechanism: Points = minutes x shot attempts per minute x points per attempt + FT. Attempts depend on usage and role (stable but changing with teammates), efficiency on shot quality, opponent defense style and shooting regression; minutes on foul trouble and blowouts. Teammate absences concentrate shots on remaining scorers in short rotations; tempo scales attempts.

interactions.hypothesis: Absence of the primary scorer raises usage but lowers efficiency; effect depends on whether the replacement is a same-role scorer.
Zone defense lowers drive-based scoring and raises three-point attempts, changing scoring distribution by role.
High rungs are sensitive to the probability of a lopsided game; mixture model is required.
Fast tempo increases attempts but late fouls matter more in tight games for FT points.

When a primary scorer is out, a remaining scorer's usage rises but his efficiency falls because the extra shots are lower quality and defences key on him; the net points gain flattens (or even reverses) as usage climbs beyond about 28 percent, particularly if the replacement is not a same-role scorer.
interactions.how_to_test: Using games with a missing top scorer compare player points per shot at baseline usage and at high usage; fit points = usage * efficiency(usage) and test for concavity.

interactions.hypothesis: For a starter on a favourite, the chance of crossing a high points rung is dominated by the probability of staying in a competitive game; in the blowout regime minutes drop by about 8 and points by about 6, so the high rung is a mixture and lower rungs are relatively insensitive.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare probability of 20 plus points among starters in games with predicted margin above and below 12, holding usage fixed; the gap should be larger at high rungs than at lower rungs.

interactions.hypothesis: Attempts equal usage share times team possessions, so a high-usage player in a fast game has a multiplicative boost to volume and variance, in a way that an additive tempo term cannot capture for large usage.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress player FGA on tempo, usage and their product, using games from the previous two seasons, and compare against the no-product model.

interactions.hypothesis: Late free throws accrue only if the game stays within about six points inside the last two minutes and only to the ball handlers on the floor, so the contribution is a step function of closeness times role, nearly zero for bigs and for blowouts.
interactions.how_to_test: Bucket games by margin at 2:00 and compare late free throws by position; confirm a step in the 0-6 point bucket for guards.

interactions.hypothesis: The weight on observed shooting streaks relative to the shot-location expectation should fall as the number of attempts grows and rise when the player's shot mix changed (new role or new team), so the regression target is conditional on sample size and on role change.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare out-of-sample prediction of next-game points per attempt using observed-only, xPPS-only and blended estimates stratified by attempts to date and by role change flags.

nonlinearities.shape: bimodal mixture with a threshold in expected margin: minutes drop sharply beyond a lead of about 15
nonlinearities.why: Points are nearly proportional to minutes, but minutes are not a smooth function of the spread; the jump between a competitive game and a bench-clearing blowout creates a discontinuity in the probability of reaching high rungs.

nonlinearities.shape: step at two first-half fouls and again at four total fouls, coach-dependent
nonlinearities.why: A second foul before halftime usually produces an immediate benching and a third a longer one, so lost minutes jump rather than rising proportionally to the foul rate, creating a heavy left tail in minutes and points.

nonlinearities.shape: concave: usage gain with falling efficiency, saturating around high usage
nonlinearities.why: The first extra shots come at near baseline quality, later ones are contested attempts, so marginal points per extra attempt decline; a linear usage-redistribution model overstates the remaining scorers' production when a star is out.

mechanism_review.summary: Points are minutes times shot attempts per minute times points per attempt plus free-throw points, a chain in which each stage is stochastic and several are strongly coupled to the game's script. Whether and how long the player plays is a mixture: availability (DNP, minute restrictions), foul trouble (a threshold event), and blowout truncation that makes minutes bimodal for starters on heavy favourites. Shot volume follows usage, pace and the teammates on the floor (absences redistribute shots to remaining scorers at lower efficiency), and conversion depends on shot quality, opponent defence, and a large luck component that should be shrunk hard to talent over 30 games. Late free throws in close games add points for ball handlers. The result is an overdispersed integer distribution with a zero or very low component for non-participation, a heavy right tail from hot nights, and contract rungs (such as 25+ points) that sit in that tail.

stages.name: Participation: plays, starts, or does not
stages.description: Before any rate matters, the player must be on the floor. College teams publish little injury information, so a starter's status is often learned at warm-ups, and transfers or eligibility issues can change a roster without notice. The scenario set is {plays full role, plays restricted, does not play}, and the settlement rule for a non-appearance decides whether this stage is a void or a NO.
stages.distribution: Mixture with a small point mass at zero (DNP, typically 3 to 8 percent for a listed starter in a long season) and a restricted-minutes component for players returning from injury.

stages.name: Minutes as a state-dependent distribution
stages.description: Starters average 28 to 35 minutes but the realised minutes depend on the game state: in a blowout starters sit after about 30 to 32 minutes of lead time, in a close game they play 36 or more, and early foul trouble (two in the first half, four in the second) cuts minutes by a coach-specific rule. The expected minutes are therefore not a single number but a mixture whose weights depend on the spread and on foul risk, so a high points rung is much more sensitive to the probability of a competitive game than the mean suggests.
stages.distribution: Minutes are bimodal for stars on big favourites (about 25 versus 34), truncated at 40 plus overtime; foul trouble creates a long left tail.

stages.name: Shot attempts per minute: usage, pace and teammates
stages.description: Field-goal attempts per minute equal the player's usage share of team possessions times the game's pace, redistributed by who else is on the floor. When a primary scorer is out, remaining scorers take more shots but at lower efficiency because the shots are harder, and the effect depends on whether the replacement is a same-role scorer or a different type. Opponent style (zone versus man) changes the shot distribution by role.
stages.distribution: Shot count per game is overdispersed relative to Poisson (variance about 1.5 to 2 times mean), and strongly correlated with minutes and with team pace.

stages.name: Conversion: points per attempt with large luck
stages.description: Points per attempt depend on shot mix (rim, mid-range, three-point), shot quality and the opponent's defence, but a large part of a player's season percentage is luck: three-point percentage over 150 attempts has a sampling sd near 4 percentage points, comparable to real differences between shooters. The right expected conversion is a shrunk estimate that combines the player's own record, his shot locations and a prior by role.
stages.distribution: Binomial-like conversion with hierarchical shrinkage; per-game points per attempt has an sd of 0.25 to 0.35, much of it unforecastable.

stages.name: Free-throw trips and late-game script
stages.description: Free-throw points come from drawn fouls during play and from the closing minutes of close games when the trailing team fouls and ball handlers take the shots. A guard on a team leading in a close game can add 4 to 8 points in the last two minutes. The trips depend on the player's drawn-foul rate against the opponent's foul propensity and on whether the game is within reach. This part of the distribution is a heavy tail from close games, not a smooth rate.
stages.distribution: Free-throw attempts per game for a guard are overdispersed with a zero-inflated closing component; FT% per game has an sd near 15 points.

stages.name: Count distribution and settlement
stages.description: The player's points are an integer total with a variance greater than a Poisson of the same mean because the stages above are positively correlated (minutes drive attempts drive points), plus the participation mixture. High rungs depend on the tail shape, and the correlation of points with game total and margin matters if the contract is part of a parlay. The Race-to-N series, first-passage events, are no longer part of this archetype (moved to unreg:race_to_n_points), so cbb.race_early_scoring_profile is not a stage input here.
stages.distribution: Overdispersed negative-binomial-like integer count with a mass at zero from non-participation and a heavy right tail from hot shooting nights.

talent_strength.note: Player scoring talent is estimated from usage and shrunk conversion; opponent-adjusted team ratings are not attached to this archetype.

opponent_matchup.note: Opponent scheme (zone, press) shifts shot types by role; role-specific points-allowed (cbb.opp_stat_allowed) was dropped as too sparse, so matchup evidence here is thin and the effect on one player's points is small.

role_personnel.note: Usage, redistribution and minutes scenarios are the core of the prop.

availability_news.note: Status and DNP risk; the settlement rule determines whether availability is a label issue (NO) or only an information issue (void).

coaching_scheme.note: Coach rules on foul benching and bench clearing set the left and right tails of minutes.

environment.note: Venue and altitude effects on one player's points are small compared with the 6 to 8 point per-game sd and are absorbed by team pace and home-court shifts in the team inputs; no player-specific environment signal is known.

game_context_script.note: Game state truncates starters' minutes in blowouts and creates late free-throw trips in close games.

pace_volume.note: Attempts scale with possessions; the shared game pace is the same for both teams.

efficiency_conversion.note: Shrunk conversion on a location-based expectation.

distribution_variance.note: Overdispersed integer outcome; the stat_dist input exists in the catalog but is not attached to this archetype.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest and schedule density effects on an individual's scoring are small and cannot be separated from noise for a single game; the main schedule effect, rotation changes in blowout-prone games, is handled in the script stage.

officiating_rules.note: Crew whistle tendency affects drawn fouls and free-throw trips; the crew is usually unknown pregame.

contract_review.settlement_definition: After the market-universe reconciliation no live series is attached to this key: the four 'Race to N Points' series (KXNCAAMBFIRST10, FIRST25, FIRST50, RACE) were moved to the new archetype unreg:race_to_n_points, and no per-player points ladder exists in the ledger. The archetype target is a player's points over a half-point or N+ strike, which would settle on the official box score of the named game; whether regulation only or overtime counts, what a player who does not play (DNP) does to the market (void or NO), and the source of the player statistic are not visible. All statements about rungs, DNP rates and strike construction in this record are therefore conditional on such a contract appearing.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: No live series, so no rules text names a source. Likely the official box score (NCAA or school statistician), with ESPN/Sports-Reference as secondary, but the rules do not say so; box-score corrections after the final can change a player's points by one or two.
variants_and_edge_cases: A player points-over strike is a count threshold on a discrete variable (integer, overdispersed); rung spacing and whether 'N+' or 'over N.5' construction is used cannot be verified.

DNP handling is the first-order unknown for any player prop: if a DNP resolves to NO rather than void, availability probability is a multiplicative term in every YES price; if void, availability drops out of the label but not the information set.
Overtime: a game that goes to extra time adds about 3 to 4 points to a starter's expected total in 5 to 6 percent of games; whether these count is not stated.
College rosters can add or remove a player for non-injury reasons (eligibility rulings, suspension, transfer) between listing and tip, which behaves like a DNP with little warning.

interactions.hypothesis: Rebounds scale with the pool times minutes share; fast, poorly shooting games lift everyone.
A missing finisher lowers assists via conversion; a missing creator raises the remaining guard's assists.
Zone defenses leak offensive rebounds to opponents, boosting rebounding opportunities for the crashing team's bigs.
Blowout probability widens the left tail; use a minutes mixture to calibrate rung probabilities.

Rebounds equal the pool per minute times minutes times the player's share, so a game with many misses (slow, poor shooting) multiplies the effect of extra minutes; in a blowout where the pool is the same but minutes drop, the missed-shot supply no longer helps a starter who is sitting.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress player rebounds on expected pool, expected minutes and their product, using starters in prior seasons, and compare to an additive form.

interactions.hypothesis: The effect of a teammate's absence on a guard's assists depends on the absent player's role: a missing finisher lowers conversion of the guard's passes and so his assists, while a missing creator hands him more passes; the same input has opposite signs.
interactions.how_to_test: Split with/without games by the absent player's role (creator versus finisher) and compare the change in the guard's assists per 40.

interactions.hypothesis: Zone defences keep bigs away from the basket and give up offensive rebounds to the crashing team, so the rebounding advantage of a larger team against a zone is larger than against man defence, in games where the offence is willing to crash.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate offensive rebound percentage in games against zone-heavy opponents versus others, interacted with the team's height and crash tendency.

interactions.hypothesis: One shooting shock raises a guard's assists and lowers his rebounds, so a combined threshold has a narrower distribution than independent marginals imply, in the middle, while single-stat tails remain wide; this is a joint distribution feature, not a mean shift.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute the empirical correlation of residual rebounds and assists for guards and compare simulated and observed probabilities of exceeding combined thresholds.

interactions.hypothesis: When a co-starting big is out, the other big's rebound share rises by a fraction of the absent player's share, but only if the replacement is smaller; if the replacement is another big the effect is small, and this conditional logic depends on who the replacement is and not only on the absence.
interactions.how_to_test: Using games with a missing big, compare rebounds per 40 of the remaining big by replacement type (big versus wing) after controlling for opponent size.

nonlinearities.shape: diminishing returns in the height and weight gap, with saturation beyond about 3 inches per matchup
nonlinearities.why: Share gains from a size advantage flatten once positioning and boxing out are secured, so a linear size-gap term overstates the rebounding of very tall players against average opposition.

nonlinearities.shape: convex in creation share for primary handlers, low and flat for non-handlers
nonlinearities.why: Assists concentrate in the one or two players who start possessions; the step between primary and secondary handler is much larger than the difference in raw passing skill suggests, producing a discontinuity by role.

nonlinearities.shape: stat-specific threshold: minutes cuts start at lower lead margins for guards (assists) than for bigs (rebounds)
nonlinearities.why: Coaches typically pull the guards who run the offence earlier and leave rebounders in to protect the glass, so the high-rung probabilities for assists fall faster with expected margin than those for rebounds.

mechanism_review.summary: Rebounds and assists are the two stats in which a player's production depends mostly on what teammates and opponents do, not on his own shooting. A rebound is a share of a finite pool of misses (both teams' misses, split offensive and defensive), with the player's share determined by who else is on the floor competing for the same boards, his positioning and the location and length of the missed shots; an assist is a credit for a teammate's made basket, so it is the product of the player's opportunity to create (ball-handling share), teammates' shot-making (largely luck game to game) and the scorer's discretion. Both scale with minutes and pace, and both move in opposite directions with game shooting luck (hot shooting means fewer rebounds and more assists), which makes the two stats a negatively dependent pair and gives each a different sensitivity to blowouts and lineup changes than points.

stages.name: Minutes and the lineup he shares the floor with
stages.description: Both stats are earned during minutes on the floor, but what matters for rebounds is who else is there: two bigs split the boards while one big alone collects them, and a small-ball unit gives guards more rebounding chances. For assists, whether the player or a teammate is the primary handler on the floor controls the creation share. Minutes themselves are truncated by foul trouble and blowouts, and lineups shift when a starter is missing.
stages.distribution: Minutes as a bounded mixture (blowout, foul trouble); lineup composition is a discrete set of the team's common five-man units with probabilities depending on availability.

stages.name: Supply of rebounds: misses, their location and who collects
stages.description: The pool is total missed field goals and live missed free throws by both teams in the minutes played, which rises with pace and with poor shooting. The split between offensive and defensive rebounds depends on the teams' crashing versus getting back philosophy. The location of the miss matters: long three-point misses carry the ball farther and favour guards and wings, rim misses favour bigs. A team facing a zone gives up different rebounding geometry than against man defence.
stages.distribution: Rebound pool per game is approximately normal around 60 to 70 total opportunities with an sd of about 7, the player's share is a Dirichlet-like split with sd from lineup and positioning.

stages.name: Player rebounding share against teammates and opponents
stages.description: A player's rebound rate (share of available boards while on the floor) depends on size, positioning, effort and opponent size, but it is capped by the competition from teammates on the floor and by the opponent's physical matchup. Rate estimates from 30 games have meaningful sampling error, especially for offensive rebounds which are rare events.
stages.distribution: Rebound rate per minute is stable across seasons for bigs (reliable) and noisy for guards; offensive rebounds approximately Poisson with a mean of about 1 for a rotation big.

stages.name: Assist creation: opportunity times teammate conversion
stages.description: An assist requires a teammate to score after the player's pass. The potential-assist volume depends on the player's share of ball handling and pick-and-roll initiation; conversion depends on teammate shot quality and make rates, which are luck-dominated game by game and shape which shot types (three-pointers and dunks are far more often assisted than isolation twos). When a creator is missing, the other guards' assists rise but with fewer finishers they lose conversion, and when a finisher is missing, the creator's assists fall.
stages.distribution: Assists are overdispersed with variance about 1.4 to 1.8 times the mean; strongly dependent on the number of team made field goals (correlation of about 0.5 between a guard's assists and team makes).

stages.name: Shared game-level shooting shock
stages.description: A single latent factor, how well both teams shoot in this game, enters both stats with opposite signs: more makes mean more assists and fewer rebounds, fewer makes mean more rebounds. This shock is mostly luck, so it is a source of variance and of negative dependence between the two stats for the same player and between players on the same team.
stages.distribution: Shared shock with a loading near +0.6 on assists and about -0.5 on rebounds for guards; the sd of team field-goal percentage in a game is about 7 percentage points.

stages.name: Count distribution, recording and contract
stages.description: The counts are non-negative integers with overdispersion and a mass near zero for low-minute players. The recorded value depends on the official statistician for assists and on team versus individual credit for rebounds. Ladder rungs for a combination stat integrate two correlated counts. Contract details (DNP handling, overtime) are undefined because no series exists.
stages.distribution: Negative binomial for each stat with a negative copula between them; measurement noise of about one unit for assists in a few percent of games.

talent_strength.note: Player rebounding rate and assist creation rate by role; stable for bigs' rebounds and weaker for guards' assists.

opponent_matchup.note: Opponent size, scheme and the shot-location mix of misses.

role_personnel.note: Who else is on the floor governs both rebound competition and creation share.

availability_news.note: Player and teammates; the creator-versus-finisher distinction decides the sign of the assist effect.

coaching_scheme.note: Crashing the offensive glass versus transition defence, and zone or man schemes, are coaching choices.

environment.note: Altitude and arena conditions change team shooting and pace slightly but have no separate effect on rebound share or assist credit known beyond the pace and scorekeeper terms; none is modelled as its own input.

game_context_script.note: Blowouts truncate starters' minutes; rebounders tend to stay in longer than scorers, so the stat-specific truncation differs.

pace_volume.note: Possessions and misses supply the rebound pool; made baskets supply the assist pool.

efficiency_conversion.note: Teammate shot-making is luck-dominated and enters assists directly. Assists depend on the regressed make rates of the teammates who receive passes, so cbb.player_shooting_regression (applied to recipients) and team-level cbb.three_pt_luck are attached in addition to the shared shock factor.

distribution_variance.note: Overdispersed counts with a negative dependence between rebounds and assists.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest, travel and rivalry effects on a player's rebounds or assists are below the per-game noise of these counts and no mechanism specific to either stat is known; any schedule-driven rotation change is captured by minutes.

officiating_rules.note: Official scorer judgement on assists and rebound credit (home statistician) is the officiating-type effect for these stats, and no attached input measures it; the box-score source input is attached only to the generic props archetype.

settlement_contract.note: No live series, no rules text; DNP, overtime, combination definition and statistician source are undefined, so label rules cannot be audited.

Treatment of a non-appearance, of overtime, of how a combination is summed, and of which statistician or provider is authoritative cannot be established from any sampled text and is therefore unverified; it is not assumed to match the points or full-game series.

Official NCAA box score from the home statistician is the likely source; provider differences for assists and rebounds are a documented issue in college where volunteer or student statisticians are used at smaller programmes (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED for magnitude).
variants_and_edge_cases: Rebounds in college box scores include offensive and defensive rebounds by the player but team rebounds (deadball, shot-clock violations) are credited to the team, so total board counts differ across providers by whether team rebounds are included in the team line.

Assists are a judgement of the official scorer (a pass leading directly to a basket), with a recognised range of scorer discretion between venues; an assist threshold such as 7.5 is therefore sensitive to who keeps the book.

A rebounds-plus-assists combination couples two stats that are negatively related through game shooting (hot shooting lifts assists, lowers rebounds), so the combination variance is lower than the sum of variances for guards.
Overtime adds about five minutes of play for the starters in 5 to 6 percent of games, lifting expected counts by about 12 to 15 percent in those games; whether overtime counts is undefined.

Single-game outcomes are luck-dominated; value lies in volume, minutes and availability rather than in 3P% trends.

Gives a shot-quality-based target for the three-point make rate so that streaks in 3P% are regressed correctly. History window: use seasons from 2019-20 onward for the league make-rate level because the men's three-point line moved to the international distance in 2019-20; earlier seasons inform player skill only after re-basing to the league mean.

interactions.hypothesis: Attempts per minute times minutes sets attempts; minute risk matters more than make rate drift.
Zone-heavy opponents concede threes, raising attempts for spot-up shooters.
Shrinkage should depend on attempts to date; early-season hot shooters are overpriced.

Expected attempts equal attempts per minute times minutes, but the variances of the two multiply into an even larger relative spread in attempts for shooters with short and uncertain minutes, so the same average attempts line has fatter tails for rotation shooters than for starters.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare dispersion of attempts per game between starters and bench shooters at equal mean attempts, and test a model with a shared minutes shock.

interactions.hypothesis: A zone defence that concedes perimeter looks raises attempts for stationary spot-up shooters more than for creators, who face the same zone with less advantage; the effect of scheme therefore depends on the shooter's role.
interactions.how_to_test: Split shooter games by opponent zone share terciles and by assisted-three share, and compare attempts per 40 changes.

interactions.hypothesis: Each additional attempt in the sample adds less weight to the player's own rate in the posterior than the previous one, so the effect of hot streaks on forecast make probability flattens with accumulated attempts; early-season hot shooters are over-weighted if weights are linear in games instead of attempts.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare out-of-sample forecasts for the next 10 games from estimators with shrinkage constant tied to attempts versus tied to games, by attempts to date buckets.

interactions.hypothesis: A missing primary creator reduces catch-and-shoot attempts for shooters who depend on that creator's passes and raises off-dribble attempts at lower make rates for shooters who can create for themselves; the sign of the net change in made threes depends on the shooter's assisted share.
interactions.how_to_test: From with/without data, regress the change in made threes per 40 on the shooter's assisted share and the absent creator's assist share.

interactions.hypothesis: For a favourite's shooter a blowout means fewer minutes and few late attempts, while for an underdog's shooter the same game means garbage-time attempts at low quality; the game-state regime changes both the volume and the make probability with opposite signs for the two sides.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare threes attempted and made per 40 for the winning and losing team's shooters in games decided by 15 or more points.

nonlinearities.shape: hyperbolic shrinkage weight n/(n+k) in attempts, with k near 80 to 120
nonlinearities.why: Make rate on small samples is almost pure noise and on large samples is informative, so the weight on a player's own percentage rises concavely with attempts; a constant weight misprices early-season hot shooters and freshman shooters.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold-driven mass: P(0 makes) decays roughly geometrically with attempts and jumps for players with fewer than 3 expected attempts
nonlinearities.why: For low-volume shooters the zero rung carries large probability and is sensitive to a one-attempt change in the mean, which is a non-linear region of the cumulative distribution that a normal approximation cannot represent.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating in minutes above about 32 and linear below
nonlinearities.why: Attempts per game plateau for high-volume starters because shot-clock cycles, and plays designed for others, cap the number of attempts, so extra minutes beyond a point add fewer threes than the per-40 rate implies.

mechanism_review.summary: Threes made equals the number of three-point attempts times the make probability on each, where attempts are a volume process driven by minutes, role, teammates' ability to create catch-and-shoot looks, opponent scheme and game script (trailing teams shoot more threes), and the make probability is shot-quality and skill, shrunk heavily because college samples of 100 to 200 attempts leave a sampling sd of about 3.5 to 4.5 percentage points, comparable to true differences between shooters. The outcome is therefore a thinned count with uncertainty in both the thinning probability and the attempt rate, so rung probabilities are far more dispersed than a Poisson with the same mean, and edges, if any, come from volume and minutes (forecastable) rather than from make rate (mostly luck).

stages.name: Participation and minutes for the shooter
stages.description: A shooter's expected attempts require him to play, and minutes are a mixture: starters on large favourites are removed in blowouts, and foul trouble reduces minutes in a discrete fashion. Role specialists (spot-up shooters) often play fewer minutes and are more exposed to rotation decisions, so the minute uncertainty has a bigger relative effect on their attempts than for a primary scorer.
stages.distribution: Minutes as a truncated mixture; probability of 20 or fewer minutes for a starter on a favourite can be 20 to 30 percent.

stages.name: Attempt volume from role and the creation of open looks
stages.description: Three-point attempts per minute depend on the player's role (stretch big, spot-up wing, creator), the share of his threes that are assisted catch-and-shoot attempts and thus depend on who creates for him, and the team's scheme. When a primary creator is out, assisted catch-and-shoot threes for the remaining shooters fall, while off-dribble threes rise if the shooter becomes the handler. Pace scales opportunities.
stages.distribution: Attempts per game are overdispersed relative to Poisson (variance about 1.5 times the mean), correlated with minutes and with the number of team possessions.

stages.name: Opponent scheme: volume conceded versus percentage conceded
stages.description: Opponent three-point defence has two parts with very different persistence: the rate of three-point attempts a defence concedes (scheme, zone, pack-line, closeout style) is a persistent trait that changes the shooter's attempts, while the three-point percentage it allows is mostly luck over a season and regresses almost entirely to the mean. A zone that concedes threes raises attempts for spot-up shooters; a pressing, switching defence lowers them.
stages.distribution: Opponent attempts-allowed rate has a season-to-season correlation of about 0.5 to 0.6 (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED) while percentage allowed has near-zero persistence.

stages.name: Game script: trailing teams shoot more threes
stages.description: Three-point attempts rise when a team is trailing late and falls when it leads comfortably, since the trailing team needs possessions worth three points and the leading team runs the clock. This ties the shooter's attempts to the probability distribution of the game's margin: underdog shooters gain late attempts, favourite shooters lose minutes. The effect interacts with the blowout stage because garbage-time threes are high-volume but low-quality.
stages.distribution: Late-game attempt rate increases by about 15 to 30 percent for the trailing team in the final five minutes (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED magnitude); a small right tail of garbage-time attempts.

stages.name: Make probability: shot quality, skill and heavy regression
stages.description: The probability that an attempt is made depends on shot type (open catch-and-shoot versus contested off-dribble), distance beyond the line, player skill and defender proximity. A single season's percentage is a noisy measure: a 38 percent shooter on 150 attempts has a 95 percent interval of roughly 30 to 46 percent, so the estimate must be a shrunk posterior combining the player's record, the free-throw percentage as a skill proxy and the shot-quality context.
stages.distribution: Posterior Beta distribution for p with an effective prior of about 80 to 120 attempts; game-level Binomial variance adds an sd of about 1.2 makes for six attempts.

stages.name: Compound distribution and ladder mapping
stages.description: The count of makes is the compound of the attempts distribution, the minute mixture and the Beta-uncertain make probability; rung probabilities are read from the compound's cumulative distribution. The zero rung is dominated by low-attempt games, the upper rungs by hot streaks. Contract specifics are unknown, so any rung beyond the first cannot be tied to rules.
stages.distribution: Beta-binomial compound with a negative-binomial attempts mixture and a zero-inflated minute component; overdispersion index of about 1.3 to 1.6 relative to a plain Binomial.

talent_strength.note: Shooting skill with heavy shrinkage and a shot-quality expectation.

opponent_matchup.note: Attempt conceded rates persist, percentages allowed do not; the split decides how much to use.

role_personnel.note: Spot-up versus creator role and the dependence on teammates' assists.

availability_news.note: Own availability and creators' availability both matter; disclosure thin.

coaching_scheme.note: Coach schemes drive the team's three-point attempt rate and the opponent's scheme drives the conceded rate.

environment.note: Arena conditions (sight lines, backgrounds, altitude) are sometimes cited for shooting but no robust, venue-level effect on three-point percentage separate from the home edge is known, and the shooter's own rate dominates.

game_context_script.note: Trailing teams take more threes and starters on favourites sit in blowouts.

efficiency_conversion.note: Luck versus skill split is the central estimation problem.

distribution_variance.note: Compound distribution with attempts and make uncertainty.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Rest, travel and rivalry effects on a single shooter's attempt volume or percentage are far below the game-to-game shooting noise and no shooting-specific schedule effect has been shown in college data.

officiating_rules.note: Officials' whistle influences free throws and fouls but not whether a three-point attempt is made or counted; the stat is an objective event with minimal scorer discretion.

settlement_contract.note: No live series or rules text exists for single-game threes made, so DNP handling, overtime and the source of truth are undefined and cannot be audited.

contract_review.settlement_definition: No live Kalshi series exists in the ledger for single-game college three-pointers made, so there is no rules text to read. The intended contract is one named player's three-point field goals made in one game over a half-point or integer threshold, settled from the official box score; the three-point line in men's college basketball is at the international distance, so a made shot counts three points and is recorded as 3PM. What a DNP does to the market, whether overtime counts, and which provider is authoritative are unspecified. The season-long stat-leader series for threes made per game in the unregistered archetype is a different contract and is not evidence for this one.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Undefined; official NCAA box score is the likely source. Three-point makes are objective events, so measurement error is smaller than for assists, but late corrections of a made two versus three are possible.
variants_and_edge_cases: Threes made is a compound count: attempts (a non-negative integer with its own variance) thinned by a make probability, so the zero, one and two-plus rungs have strongly different sensitivities to attempts versus make rate.

Rungs such as '3 or more' sit in the upper tail for most players (a volume shooter attempts about 6 to 8 and makes 35 to 40 percent), where hot-shooting nights dominate and luck is the main determinant.
A player with fewer than five attempts in a blowout or in foul trouble can produce zero even with a good rate; low-minute appearances create a heavy zero mass.
Overtime adds an expected 1 to 2 attempts for a high-volume shooter in the 5 to 6 percent of games that go to extra time; whether those count is undefined.

The men's college three-point line moved to the international distance in 2019-20, so league three-point make rates before and after differ; any prior-season make-rate history must be re-based to the league level of its season.

Before Selection Sunday it integrates over seed and region uncertainty; afterward it follows the actual path. Star injury risk and path matchups dominate the tails; markets include brand bias and long-shot bias.

interactions.hypothesis: Title odds are convex in rating and sensitive to single-game variance; high-variance teams are mispriced when ratings alone are used.
Pre-bracket futures integrate over seed/region assignment, which resolves at Selection Sunday.
A single star injury changes title odds by large factors; mixture models matter.
Brand teams may be overpriced vs the book consensus; test the gap by popularity.

Title probability is a product over six games of win probabilities that are probit in rating gap over game sd, so the log-title probability is approximately linear in rating gap and its sensitivity to game sd is largest for the favourite: a modest increase in game variance transfers a large share of title equity from the best team to the field.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate the field with sd 9, 10.5 and 12 and compare the shift in the top team's title probability, then check historical top-seed title frequency against the sd that matches it.

interactions.hypothesis: Title and qualification probabilities for a bubble or low-seed team depend on the field size and play-in structure: in an expanded field an extra play-in win may be required for the lowest seeds, and the allocation of bids changes who is in at all, so the simulator output is conditional on the format.
interactions.how_to_test: Run the bracket simulator under 68-team and 76-team structures with identical ratings and compare title and qualification probabilities for teams ranked 40 to 80.

interactions.hypothesis: The loss of one top player cuts strength by an amount that depends on the replacement and the team's depth; combined with the number of rounds (each with an independent miss probability) the strength distribution of a title contender is a mixture whose lower component holds nontrivial weight, and the favourite's title probability is the weighted sum over states.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute title probability for a top team under a no-injury state and under a star-out state and mix with per-game miss probabilities; compare to a model that uses average strength.

interactions.hypothesis: A top seed with a double bye plays one fewer game and has an extra rest day, while a lower seed must win four games in four days; the advantage of a bye grows with the length of the bracket and with how thin the team's rotation is, so the fatigue effect depends on the format.
interactions.how_to_test: Using past conference tournaments compare win rates of seeds by number of games needed and rotation depth after controlling for rating.

interactions.hypothesis: Because title probability is convex in strength, adding uncertainty about March strength raises the title probability of mid-tier contenders and lowers the favourite's (Jensen's inequality on the exponential-like tail), so the same current rating gap yields different odds in November and in February.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute title odds of the same team with sd 0, 1.5 and 3 for March rating and compare with the historical frequency by preseason rank.

interactions.hypothesis: The men's and women's tournaments share no games or players, so the combo probability is the product of the two title probabilities; the product makes a combo of two favourites far less likely than either leg, and any shared shock (a school-wide event) would be a small positive correlation only.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare historical combo-implied probabilities from the two marginal models with the product rule and test for dependence between men's and women's champions' pre-tournament rating ranks.

interactions.hypothesis: In a November event most of a team's rating is still preseason prior, so the event's format matters more when that prior is uncertain: pool play seeded by point differential amplifies rating error into seeding error, while a straight bracket only compounds per-game error.
interactions.how_to_test: Backtest event champion log-loss by format type, splitting teams by preseason-prior weight (returning minutes share) at the event date.

nonlinearities.shape: exponential-like convexity of title probability in rating gap (product of six probit terms)
nonlinearities.why: A one point rating edge raises each round's win probability by about 3 percentage points near 50 percent, which compounds into a title probability that rises several-fold; a linear model on rating cannot reproduce the tail concentration at the top.

nonlinearities.shape: variance grows with horizon (sqrt time) and the mean reverts toward the league mean
nonlinearities.why: A November rating overstates how far a team will stand from average in March, so the best and worst teams revert; the sd of change is larger for new rosters, making the horizon effect conditional on roster continuity.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating effect on title probability beyond a game sd of about 12 points
nonlinearities.why: Once the game sd is already large, additional variance shifts title equity from the favourite to the field by progressively less, since probabilities approach a floor determined by bracket structure.

mechanism_review.summary: A title is a product of survival probabilities across a single-elimination bracket whose structure is revealed only on Selection Sunday, and whose team strengths are themselves uncertain months in advance. For the national title, probability equals the chance of reaching the field times the chance of winning six (or seven for play-in teams) neutral-site games, each given by the rating gap through a link with a spread sd of about 10 to 11 points, so small edges compound convexly: a team 3 points better than its competition in each round has a title probability several times that of a team 1 point better. Before the bracket exists the model must integrate over the seed and region assignment, the injury state of stars in March, and the drift of strength between now and then. The NIT, the Crown and November in-season events run the same survival logic on smaller fields with their own selection and format rules, conference-of-champion buckets sum title probability over affiliated teams, and the men's-and-women's combo multiplies in a separate women's title probability.

stages.name: Team strength distribution in March, not today
stages.description: A title market opened in November is priced on the strength a team will have in March, which differs from current strength through player development, rotation settling, transfers' integration and injuries; the drift has an sd of several rating points by March for young or churned rosters. The right object is a distribution over March strength, which then goes into the bracket integration, and the spread of that distribution determines how fat the title tail is.
stages.distribution: Random-walk-like innovation in team rating with sd growing as sqrt(time) plus discrete injury jumps; March rating sd about 2 to 3 points of adjusted margin for November pricing, falling to about 1 point by February.

stages.name: Making the field, seed and region
stages.description: Before Selection Sunday a team must earn a place (by conference tournament title or at-large selection), receive a seed (which governs the path and the location), and be placed in a region by committee rules (avoiding same-conference early matchups, proximity placement for top seeds). The field format can change between seasons (an expanded field adds play-in games for the lowest seeds), so the number of wins a title needs is itself uncertain for bubble teams. These discrete allocations create jumps in title probability at the moment the bracket is released, so cbb.resume_metrics, cbb.auto_bid_structure and cbb.committee_ordinal_seed_model feed the seed draw here. For the NIT and Crown series the field is drawn from teams left out of the NCAA tournament, so cbb.secondary_postseason_field_model converts P(not in NCAA field) into P(in that event's field).
stages.distribution: Discrete seed assignment (1 to 16) with a distribution that is bunched around the rating-implied seed and tilted by resume; region assignment adds a categorical draw affecting path difficulty.

stages.name: Single-game win probability at neutral sites
stages.description: Each tournament game is a neutral-site game (or semi-home for pods), so no home term applies except crowd imbalance in the first weekend when a team plays near campus. The win probability equals the normal CDF of the rating gap over a game sd of about 10 to 11 points, adjusted for pace (slow underdogs shorten the game and add variance), three-point reliance and matchup styles. Empirical seed-based upset rates are a cross-check, not an additional driver, since seeds already encode ratings.
stages.distribution: Win probability as a probit link; the effective sd of margin is larger for three-point-reliant and slow teams; the match-up residual has sd about 2 points of margin per game.

stages.name: Availability and injury shocks across six rounds
stages.description: A single-elimination run lasts three weeks, during which any star's injury or illness changes strength by several points of margin; because a title needs six wins, a team has about six independent chances to be hit by an injury-weakened roster. Disclosure is poor, and an injury during the conference tournament can arrive just before Selection Sunday. The per-game probability of a star missing a game is small but, compounded over a run, is a non-trivial fraction of title equity for top teams.
stages.distribution: Mixture over player availability states with a per-game miss probability near 2 to 4 percent for each top-three player; correlated within a team through shared load and travel.

stages.name: Short brackets outside March: in-season events and leftover conference listings
stages.description: KXNCAAMBTOURNEY settles on a November multi-team event (sampled: Players Era 8) with a fixed invited field at a neutral venue over three or four days. Its champion probability depends on the event format (straight bracket or pool play with seeding by record and point differential), the draw, back-to-back fatigue, and November ratings that still carry most of the preseason prior. The title-only listings KXNCAAMBHL and KXNCAAMBSUN (conference tournaments) and KXNCAAMBBIG10REG (regular-season title) use the conference format table and the standings simulation in the same way as the conference archetype; if they duplicate the futures_conference listings they should be priced identically.
stages.distribution: Short neutral-site bracket of 2 to 4 games; champion probabilities across the 8-team field sum to one, with a top team typically at 20 to 35 percent in November given wide rating uncertainty.

stages.name: Contract mapping: title, conference buckets and cross-tournament combos
stages.description: The simulated paths settle different contracts: win-all-games for KXMARMAD, NIT, Crown and the region winner, and a sum over affiliated teams for the conference-of-champion buckets (KXNCAAMBCONF, KXMARMADCONFWIN), where affiliation is frozen at tournament start and 'Other' collects every remaining team. KXNCAAMB2ML multiplies the men's title probability by the named women's team's title probability from cbb.wcbb_title_probability. The simulation keeps joint structure so that probabilities over teams, and over conference buckets, each sum to one.
stages.distribution: Paths are exchangeable only after conditioning on the bracket; the sum over teams of title probabilities is exactly 1, and uncertainty in strength induces positive correlation among a team's own round probabilities.

talent_strength.note: March-dated strength distribution with a drift model, plus the women's title probability for the KXNCAAMB2ML leg; the two-way balance filter is not relied on (hypothesis only, see fc_balance_hypothesis).

opponent_matchup.note: Path and matchup structure by seed and region; style-specific matchup residuals are small and noisy.

role_personnel.note: Concentration of value in a few players determines how an injury changes title equity.

availability_news.note: Compounded star-injury risk over six rounds; disclosure poor.

coaching_scheme.note: Evidence that coaches add tournament wins beyond team strength is weak and confounded with roster quality, and no stable coach-specific effect size is established; rotation tendencies enter only through roster minutes.

environment.note: First- and second-round pod sites can be near some campuses and far from others; later rounds are fully neutral.

game_context_script.note: Game-level variance by style (tempo and three-point reliance) is the only script-level effect used for a season-long future.

pace_volume.note: Pace matters through the game's margin variance (slow underdogs), not through a separate volume term.

efficiency_conversion.note: Efficiency enters through the rating; a luck regression of recent shooting is inside the ratings pipeline and not a separate input.

distribution_variance.note: Fat title tails come from strength uncertainty compounded over six rounds; correlations among a team's round outcomes are induced by the shared strength draw.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Format, byes and multi-day fatigue in conference tournaments; stakes for auto-bid teams.

officiating_rules.note: Officiating crews in the tournament are assigned by the NCAA and rotate; no team-specific crew advantage or systematic crew effect on a team's advance probability is known, and crews are not known months ahead.

settlement_contract.note: Title, conference-of-champion buckets (affiliation at tournament start, 'Other' bucket), men's-and-women's combo, NIT/Crown and in-season event; vacated titles and cancelled events not addressed.
