contract_review.settlement_definition: Yes settles if the named team is the first to reach (KXNCAAMBFIRST10, KXNCAAMBFIRST25, KXNCAAMBFIRST50) or score (KXNCAAMBRACE, N in the ticker, 10 sampled) N points in the named men's college basketball game originally scheduled on the stated date. Scoring is sequential, so no tie is possible and overshooting N counts. KXNCAAMBRACE: a game postponed but starting within 48 hours stays open and settles on the official final result; cancelled or not started within 48 hours resolves to a fair price. The FIRST series samples show no postponement clause, and no sample addresses overtime or neither team reaching N.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Not named for the scoring sequence. The KXNCAAMBRACE text mentions 'the official final result' only inside its postponement clause; the FIRST series name no source. The official play-by-play is the natural source but is not stated.
variants_and_edge_cases: Two series generations: KXNCAAMBFIRST10/25/50 (one series per N, finalized samples from Apr 6, 2026) say 'first to reach N points'; KXNCAAMBRACE (active, N in the ticker, e.g. -10-UVA) says 'first to score 10 points'. Both are team-level.
The FIRST samples contain only the trademark disclaimer in rules_secondary, so they show no postponement or cancellation clause; only KXNCAAMBRACE states the 48-hour rule and fair-price resolution.

Overshoot counts: a team going from 8 to 11 on a three has reached 10. Points are scored one event at a time, so no simultaneous crossing is possible; residual risk is an official-scorer or play-by-play correction to the sequence.

N=50 can be reached after halftime for slow teams and, in very low-scoring games, only in overtime or never; no sample says whether overtime counts or how a game ending with neither team at N settles.
Both teams' markets in the same game are separate binary contracts so their prices should sum near one.

season_stat_leader.label: CBB season per-game stat leader
contract_types: Men's College Basketball Conference Stat Leader
season_stat_leader.target: Player with the highest season per-game stat (points, threes, etc.) nationally or within a conference, NCAA minimums apply
season_stat_leader.mechanism: The winner is the maximum over qualified players of a season-long per-game average accumulated over every official game, postseason included. Each average is minutes times a role-driven per-minute rate with large game-to-game noise, thinned by missed games and gated by NCAA minimum qualification, so the probability depends on talent, role stability, availability, how locked the average already is, and which official table settles it.

inputs.why: Leaderboard max-of-noisy-averages simulation including postseason games and thresholds, the direct model of this contract.
NCAA minimums decide who is eligible, so a leader near the cutoff can be removed from the contest.
Remaining-swing bound shows how locked the leaderboard is given games played and remaining.
Usage and shot share drive points, threes and rebounds per game and persist across games.
Projected minutes scale every counting stat and respond to blowouts, fouls and role.
Injury, suspension and coach decisions reduce games played and can disqualify a candidate.
Postseason and late-season availability risk for the top candidates affects both games and qualification.
Threes made per game is minutes times attempts times a Beta-uncertain make rate, the compound behind the 3PM leader markets.
Three-point attempt volume decides who can lead the made-threes category more than shooting percentage.
Rebounds per game depend on the pool of missed shots and offensive-rebound structure of the team.
Assists per game depend on the potential assists and teammates' make rate, not only the passer.
Transfers and freshmen have no college role history, so the leader pool needs cold-start priors.
Teammate injuries redistribute usage and minutes and can raise a candidate's average.
Per-game sd by role sets how quickly the average converges and how much noise remains.
Counts of games, sites and which are official define the sample size over which the average is built.
Possessions scale the opportunities for counting stats and differ by team across the pool.
Stat provider reliability and correction lag matter for the final official table.
Wording fixes which games count and the minimum thresholds and the non-qualification clause.
Final leader and timing of settlement from past seasons show the lag and source used.
Postseason games count, so each candidate team's expected postseason games set both the qualification denominator and the games still to average.
Settlement source is unseen; conference-office and NCAA tables can differ in minimums, games included and corrections, deciding close races.
Simulated conference tournaments and the NCAA field give the probability of each extra postseason game for a candidate's team.
Conference seeding and byes set the number of conference-tournament games each candidate can add.
Stars on heavy favourites lose minutes in blowouts all season, a systematic drag on their per-game average.
Remaining opponent strength, including soft nonconference slates, shifts per-game production systematically for a candidate.

interactions.hypothesis: Minutes and usage multiply, so a modest rise in either lifts the average more than additively, and role changes after teammate departures or injuries move leaders.
Missed games matter as a cliff once a candidate nears the NCAA minimum, so injury risk is far more costly for a leader close to the threshold.
The same gap between candidates is worth more probability late than early because each remaining game moves an average by less, so race uncertainty collapses as games are played.
A deeper team run raises the team-games denominator, so a candidate who has missed games can fall below the minimum by his team winning.

Points per game equal minutes times usage-driven per-minute scoring, so a 10 percent rise in each gives about 21 percent more, and teammate departures or injuries can raise both together for a candidate.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress player-season ppg on log minutes and log usage with an interaction and test whether the elasticity of the product is about one for each.

interactions.hypothesis: Eligibility requires a minimum share of games, so a candidate with margin of two games above the threshold who misses three loses all probability; the cost of absence is zero until the threshold and then total.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate candidates with and without the filter and compare leader probability for players within 3 games of the minimum.

interactions.hypothesis: Early in the season an average moves by up to a point per game and leaders change often; after 25 games it moves by less than a few tenths, so the probability a leader holds rises sharply in the second half of the season.
interactions.how_to_test: Calibrate historical leader probability at game 10, 20 and 30 against the realised leader and check the lead-hold rate by z-score bucket.

interactions.hypothesis: Made threes are attempts times a noisy make rate; volume gives a stable base and the make rate adds luck, so the 3PM leader is typically a high-volume shooter whose make rate is not extreme and uncertainty is dominated by the rate for low-volume candidates.
interactions.how_to_test: Decompose season 3PM leaders into volume and percentage in past seasons and check which component explains the leader rank change between week 8 and the end.

interactions.hypothesis: A leader on a deep-run team gains postseason games that reduce noise but raise injury exposure, and a leader on an early-eliminated team stops accumulating games, so the effect of tournament depth depends on both the quality of opposition and risk of absence.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare changes in per-game average between the end of the regular season and the final for leaders by postseason games played.

interactions.hypothesis: Postseason games raise the team-games denominator, so a candidate who has already missed games can lose qualification because his team keeps winning, while extra games also dilute a hot start; the effect exists only for candidates near the minimum.
interactions.how_to_test: For past near-threshold leaders compute qualification status under realised versus counterfactual shorter postseason runs.

interactions.hypothesis: Expected minutes are scaled down by the share of games that become blowouts, which is highest for stars on heavy favourites, so national scoring leaders tilt toward strong players on average or weak teams.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress player-season minutes per game on team average expected margin among high-usage players; expect a negative slope beyond about 10 points.

nonlinearities.shape: decays as 1/games played (hyperbolic)
nonlinearities.why: Each game's weight in the average falls with games played, so remaining uncertainty collapses and a fixed gap is worth more probability late in the season.

nonlinearities.shape: cliff at the NCAA minimum
nonlinearities.why: Eligibility is binary; being one game short removes a candidate completely even if his average is the highest.

nonlinearities.shape: concave above about 34 minutes
nonlinearities.why: Starters near the ceiling cannot add much and foul trouble or blowouts cut minutes, so extra role gains saturate for the most used players.

mechanism_review.summary: The outcome is the argmax of a set of season-long per-game averages among players who meet NCAA minimums. A player's average equals the mean of his counting stat across all official games he plays, so it is built from minutes, role and usage, per-minute production against opponents and pace, and the count of games he is available for. Game-to-game noise is large relative to true differences between top candidates, so early in the season many players are live, and as games accumulate each new game moves the average less. Availability is a hazard: missed games shrink the sample and can drop a player under the NCAA minimum, which removes him from the contest. Postseason games add samples for deep-run teams. Each stat category has its own driver: scoring by usage, threes by attempts volume, rebounds by the missed-shot pool, assists by teammate shot making. Settlement then reads one official table.

stages.name: Candidate pool and per-game talent
stages.description: The leaderboard starts from who can plausibly lead: high-usage scorers, volume three-point shooters, big men on rebound-rich teams, primary ballhandlers, and rim protectors for blocks. Each candidate has a true per-game mean set by minutes and role, usage, per-minute production and teammates, and many of the best candidates are transfers or freshmen with no college role history, so their means are uncertain and shrunk toward role priors. National contracts have a pool of about 30 credible names; conference contracts have 5 to 10.
stages.distribution: True means are separated by a few tenths to a few points per game among the top candidates; uncertainty about each mean is large for new players and shrinks roughly as 1 over sqrt of games.

stages.name: Per-game production process
stages.description: Each game, a candidate's stat is produced from minutes, shot attempts or rebound and assist opportunities and conversion. Points are possessions times usage times efficiency plus free throws; threes made are attempts times a noisy make rate; rebounds come from the missed-shot pool; assists from teammates' shot making. Opponent strength, pace and blowout minute losses shift output systematically, not only as noise: stars on dominant teams sit more and soft schedules inflate averages.
stages.distribution: Per-game counts are overdispersed and nonnegative; points have sd near 6 to 8, threes made near 1.5 to 2 with Beta-binomial-like tails, so a season average has sd near 1 over sqrt of games times that.

stages.name: Games played, availability and postseason sample
stages.description: The average is taken over all official games the player plays: regular season, conference tournament, NCAA, NIT and other official postseason events, so the number of games depends on the team's projected postseason run, including invitational selection for the Crown, CBI or CIT. Injury, suspension or coach decisions reduce games played; the sampled rules exclude exhibition and preseason games clearly designated unofficial.
stages.distribution: Games played is a discrete count of about 28 to 38 with a left tail from injuries; missed games are clustered and correlated with team success and with the stage of the season.

stages.name: Qualification filter and race to the maximum
stages.description: Only players who meet the NCAA minimum qualification thresholds are eligible, so the winner is the maximum over the qualified set of final per-game averages. The probability for a candidate is the chance that he qualifies and that his noisy average exceeds all other qualified candidates'. Lead stability grows as games accumulate because each new game changes an average by less, and a candidate within one standard error of the leader still has a live chance.
stages.distribution: The max of several correlated noisy averages with a hard eligibility filter; probabilities concentrate on the top 2 to 4 candidates and the lead probability moves in jumps when a candidate is injured or crosses the threshold.

stages.name: Official table and settlement
stages.description: Settlement uses the player's statistics for the entire season including postseason, from some official or reference table; the sampled text is cut off at the clause about what happens if the named player does not qualify or the leader is tied, so the exact rule is not visible. Lag in official updates, differences between the NCAA site and box scores, and the treatment of non-NCAA postseason events can decide a close race.
stages.distribution: Mostly deterministic given the final table, with a small chance of source disagreement or ties that flips close races.

contract_review.settlement_data_source: Not named in the sampled text; likely the NCAA statistical leaderboards or equivalent official season statistics, to be confirmed.
variants_and_edge_cases: Conference version covers per-game stats of players in one conference across all of their games, including nonconference games ('Counts all official regular-season games, both conference and nonconference'); conference offices publish their own leaderboards, possibly with different minimums or conference-only splits, and which table settles is unseen.
Categories vary by market (points per game for SEC, made threes per game for national in the samples); other categories such as rebounds or assists were not sampled.
The sampled rules_secondary is truncated at 'If Zoom Diallo does not', so the clause on a non-qualifying or non-playing player is not visible; tie-break treatment is also not visible.
Because postseason games count, the final answer is only known after the last postseason event, and a team's postseason run changes the sample size.

coaching_and_governance_events.label: CBB next permanent head coach (Men's College Basketball Next Coach)
coaching_and_governance_events.target: Identity of the next permanent head coach named by a programme (multi-outcome, No-all if none by deadline)
coaching_and_governance_events.mechanism: The outcome is an institutional choice: a vacancy opens, an athletic director (with president, board and often a search firm) builds a candidate list from sitting head coaches, assistants and former players, ranks them on track record, ties and fit, and must win a two-sided negotiation constrained by salary, buyouts, roster budget and each candidate's own season calendar. Reports leak along the way. Settlement counts only a permanent (non-interim) hire before the deadline, so unlisted candidates and interim-only outcomes carry probability mass that all listed markets lose. The blueprint season_outcome is kept only because the catalog schema requires an existing blueprint; this archetype takes none of that blueprint's bracket or committee inputs except through the explicitly listed ones (ratings and bracket simulation are used only to score an interim coach's season and a candidate's elimination date).

inputs.why: Search stage and decision-makers bound timing and how open the candidate set still is.
Calibrated insider reports are the main information arriving during a search.
Programme-building record is how committees rank candidates.
Mass on unlisted candidates and on no permanent hire caps listed probabilities.
Alumni, former-staff and AD links are a strong prior on who is chosen.
Salary, buyout capacity and roster budget decide which candidates are reachable.
Candidate's own season or buyout dates can remove him from a fast search.
Show-cause orders and investigations remove otherwise strong candidates.
General coaching news feed captures vacancy openings and announcements with timestamps.
Point-in-time team ratings are the raw basis for a candidate's measured programme improvement.
Defines permanent versus interim, the Sep 1, 2027 cutoff and No-for-all handling.
Interim coach's results versus a fundamentals-only expectation drive the interim-to-permanent route for this vacancy.
Fundamentals-only pregame expected margins and ratings score the interim's season against expectation without any betting line.
Simulated conference finish, NCAA bid and advancement for the interim's team, and elimination dates of candidates' teams.
Preseason expectation baseline for the interim's team, needed to tell over-performance from inherited talent.
Incumbent departure hazard and succession arrangements set the no-vacancy and coach-in-waiting mass for series opened before a vacancy.

interactions.hypothesis: A finalist or offer report late in a search converts to a hire far more often than the same report in the first days after the opening.
Strong-record sitting coaches are reachable only when offer capacity covers salary plus buyout; below that ratio track record stops mattering.
A candidate still coaching in March loses probability as the transfer-portal window approaches if the school's search is already advanced.
A deferred search lets the interim's season results move his hire probability; with an immediate search they do not matter.

The same report stage converts at different rates depending on search progress: a 'finalist' report two days after a firing is often agent leverage, while one after interviews have closed with a board meeting scheduled is close to decisive.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate hire conversion by report stage split by days-since-opening and by whether a board meeting was scheduled; compare with pooled conversion. Index days by the search start, not the vacancy date, and flag vacancies with an announced deferred start.

interactions.hypothesis: Track record raises hire probability only once the school's offer capacity exceeds the candidate's salary plus buyout; below that ratio the strongest records are effectively unattainable and mass moves to assistants.
interactions.how_to_test: Logit of hire on track record interacted with an indicator offer_capacity/(salary+buyout) > 1 across past searches.

interactions.hypothesis: Searches either wait for a preferred candidate still coaching in March or close before the transfer portal opens; which regime applies depends on search age and the school's urgency, flipping the candidate's probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Among past searches with a linked candidate still alive in the NCAA tournament, compare hire rates by whether the school had announced an interim and by days to portal opening.

interactions.hypothesis: Ties scale the odds of a hire roughly proportionally at any track-record level; an alumnus with a modest record can outrank a stranger with a better one, and an AD's prior hire carries the largest multiplier.
interactions.how_to_test: Conditional logit over candidate sets with track record and tie indicators; test whether tie effects are constant on the odds scale across record quintiles.

interactions.hypothesis: Each additional credible report about listed names shrinks the unlisted mass, but the reduction slows as only late surprise hires remain; early surprises are common, late ones rare.
interactions.how_to_test: Plot fraction of hires outside the reported set against cumulative report count and days since opening across past searches.

interactions.hypothesis: With a deferred search the interim's results matter only while the search is not yet open: a strong season can cancel or shorten the search (regime A), a weak one hands the decision to a conventional search after the season (regime B), so the interim's hire probability switches level at the search start rather than varying smoothly.
interactions.how_to_test: Among past interim-led seasons, compare promotion rates for teams above and below fundamentals expectation, split by whether the school announced a search for after the season.

interactions.hypothesis: The no-hire mass and the unlisted mass are not separable: a retirement with a pre-arranged successor removes both, while a firing opens a conventional search with a large unlisted mass, so the residual masses must be mixed over departure types rather than estimated from all vacancies pooled.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate the unlisted-hire share separately for retirements with named successors, retirements without, and firings, and compare with the pooled figure.

nonlinearities.shape: convex decay in days since the search opened (flat while a deferred search has not started)
nonlinearities.why: Unlisted-candidate mass is roughly constant while the school says the search has not begun, then falls fast in the first week of the real search as names surface and flattens afterwards; a linear decay in days since the vacancy understates the unlisted mass for months in a deferred-search vacancy.

nonlinearities.shape: step function by report stage
nonlinearities.why: Conversion jumps discretely from 'linked' to 'interviewed' to 'offer' to 'agreement'; agreement reports convert near one, so the response is a staircase, not a smooth curve.

nonlinearities.shape: threshold at offer capacity equal to salary plus buyout
nonlinearities.why: Below the threshold a sitting coach is nearly unreachable; above it extra money adds little because ties and fit dominate.

nonlinearities.shape: step in promotion probability at beating expectation and NCAA bid
nonlinearities.why: Interims who finish near expectation are rarely promoted, while a clear beat plus an NCAA bid makes promotion common; the response is a rise concentrated above a performance threshold rather than proportional to wins.

mechanism_review.summary: A next-coach outcome is generated by a hiring process, not by play. A vacancy opens (firing, retirement, departure) and the athletic director, with the president or board and often a search firm, forms a candidate pool: sitting head coaches at lower-resourced or same-tier schools, top assistants and ex-player figures with ties to the programme. Candidates are ranked on programme-building record and fit, filtered by eligibility constraints, and must be reachable: salary plus their current buyout must fit the school's budget, and their own team's postseason or NBA calendar must not collide with the school's need to hire before the transfer portal. The process emits noisy reports with stage-dependent conversion. Settlement is a multi-outcome event over listed names with residual mass on unlisted hires and on no permanent hire before Sep 1, 2027.

stages.name: Vacancy and search set-up
stages.description: The cause of the opening (firing after a poor season, retirement, coach leaving for another job) determines timing, whether a successor was pre-arranged and whether an interim coach is named. The athletic director's tenure, use of a search firm and the governance chain (president, regents) determine speed and how widely the net is cast. The stage of the search at the pricing time decides how much of the outcome remains open. Public reports of 2026-10-07 (KPTV, KATU, AP via OPB) describe the sampled Oregon vacancy: Dana Altman retired effective immediately, assistant Tony Stubblefield is interim for 2026-27 and a national search is planned after the season, so the search start lags the vacancy by about five months; these facts come from news, not from the sampled rules text.
stages.distribution: Time-to-hire counted from the search start is right-skewed: in-season firings of power-conference coaches typically conclude within weeks, while a vacancy with an announced deferred search has a window of months in which no hire is expected; the pre-search window is a separate regime, not the tail of the same distribution.

stages.name: Interim season audition (deferred-search vacancies)
stages.description: When the vacancy is filled by an interim who coaches the whole season and the school defers the search, the team's results between the vacancy and the search start decide whether the interim becomes a front-runner, whether the school cancels the search, and how early or late outside candidates are contacted. The signal is performance against a fundamentals-only expectation, conference finish and NCAA advancement, not raw wins, because the roster was built by the predecessor.
stages.distribution: Mixture: a small point mass on interim-made-permanent when results beat expectation, otherwise a hard reset to a normal search after the season; the interim's probability moves in jumps with the bracket outcome.

stages.name: Candidate pool and ranking
stages.description: The plausible pool is drawn from sitting head coaches whose teams outperformed their resources, top assistants on strong staffs, and people tied to the programme or the athletic director. Ranking weighs measured improvement in adjusted efficiency, NCAA tournament success, recruiting and transfer-portal results, and ties; show-cause orders or open investigations remove names. Unlisted candidates remain possible.
stages.distribution: Probability over identities is concentrated on a few names (top two often hold most mass) with a long tail of plausible others and a non-trivial unlisted residual early in the search.

stages.name: Reachability and negotiation
stages.description: A top-ranked candidate must accept: the offer must exceed salary plus buyout at the current school, roster budget (revenue sharing and NIL) must be competitive, and the current school may counter with an extension. Candidates whose teams are still in the NCAA tournament or whose buyout drops at a later date may be unavailable when the school wants to hire. Competing vacancies at other schools bid for the same people.
stages.distribution: Acceptance is close to binary per candidate given an offer; a declined first choice shifts mass to the next names in a cascade, giving a mixture over orderings.

stages.name: Information release and settlement
stages.description: Insiders report contacts, interviews, finalists, offers and agreements; each stage has a different historical conversion to a hire, and denials carry their own signal. The university announces the hire, sometimes pending board approval. Settlement counts only a permanent coach selected before Sep 1, 2027; interim-only or unlisted outcomes settle every listed market No.
stages.distribution: Information arrives in jumps: one credible agreement report moves a candidate from tens of percent to near certainty; between reports probabilities drift slowly.

talent_strength.note: Candidate quality is the programme-building record, measured from point-in-time ratings.

opponent_matchup.note: Competing vacancies at other schools bid for the same candidates in the same window; no input tracks the simultaneous carousel and the relative attractiveness of rival openings. Stage s3 no longer claims this category; competing vacancies stay a declared gap (coach_u2).

role_personnel.note: Personnel here are the candidates and their ties to the school and the AD.

availability_news.note: Report ledger with conversion rates plus general news feed.

coaching_scheme.note: Analogue only: the athletic director's process (tenure, search firm, governance chain) plays the role of scheme; it describes how the decision is made, not any on-court scheme.

environment.note: Programme resources (salary, buyout capacity, roster budget) are the environment of the hire.

game_context_script.note: No game settles the contract, but the interim's in-season results and NCAA advancement are a path to the permanent job when an interim coaches the season before the search; irrelevant when no interim exists.

pace_volume.note: There is no count of opportunities: the event is a single hiring decision per vacancy, not an accumulation of possessions or attempts.

distribution_variance.note: Multi-outcome identity distribution with unlisted and no-hire residual mass.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Each market is one candidate for one programme (sample: Oregon men's basketball, candidate Yasir Rosemond). YES if that person is the next permanent (non-interim) head coach of the programme. Interim appointments do not count. If no permanent head coach is selected before Sep 1, 2027, every market in the event resolves No. No game, period, overtime or DNP logic applies. The rules do not name the source of truth (university announcement, board approval or signed contract) nor define the moment of 'selection'.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Not stated in the rules; in practice the university's official announcement of the permanent head coach. Kalshi's resolution source for the date of selection is unverified.
variants_and_edge_cases: Interim coach later made permanent: the rules settle on the permanent hire, so the interim's own market resolves Yes if the permanent title is conferred before Sep 1, 2027 (the sampled vacancy has an interim coaching 2026-27, so this is the main game-driven route); the transition timing and whether a removed 'interim' tag counts as 'selected' are not specified.
Hire of an unlisted person: rules do not say so explicitly, but each listed market only resolves Yes for its named person, so all listed markets would resolve No.
Agreement reported but not announced, or announced pending board approval before the cutoff and approved after it: 'selected' is undefined in the rules.
Titles such as 'head coach-in-waiting' or co-head coach are not addressed.
Only one series exists (one vacancy sampled); other programmes in the same series would share the template but different cutoff dates may apply.

Series with a sitting coach and no vacancy: the template only fixes Sep 1, 2027 as the cutoff for the Oregon event; if a future market is opened before any vacancy exists, every listed market resolves No unless a vacancy arises and is filled by the cutoff (inference from the No-for-all clause).
Coach-in-waiting or successor named before the vacancy is formal: 'selected' timing is undefined and the named person's market could settle early or on the title conferred.

overtime_periods.label: CBB overtime periods played
overtime_periods.target: Number of overtime periods played in a game (at least N OT periods)
overtime_periods.mechanism: Reaching N overtime periods requires a tied score at the end of regulation and then N-1 further ties after each five-minute period. The first tie depends on the integer pmf of the regulation margin at zero, set by the strength gap, possessions, three-point lumpiness and end-game decisions; each repeat tie depends on the short-period scoring distribution, which bonus free throws and fouled-out players from foul carryover reshape. Rungs are nested and fall geometrically.

inputs.why: Chains the regulation tie with per-period repeat-tie rates for 2+ and 3+ overtime rungs.
Fundamentals-only strength gap sets the expected margin around which tie mass is evaluated.
Expected possessions scale the margin sd; fewer possessions raise the probability of a tie.
Three-point volume makes scoring lumpier and widens the margin distribution, lowering tie mass.
Early-season rating uncertainty flattens the expected-margin distribution and raises tie probability for mismatches.
Play-for-tie versus play-for-win policy shifts tie mass only in close finishes; pooled by tier, with coach deviations only when well supported.
Foul carryover reshapes scoring in each OT period and makes repeat-tie rates period-dependent.
Intentional fouling by the trailing team changes the late margin path and the chance it ends level.
Absences move the expected margin, the only strength input to tie probability.
Home advantage shifts the expected margin away from or toward zero.
Rungs count periods played; postponement and cancellation handling are in the text.
Live score, clock, period and foul state dominate the rung probabilities once a game is tied late or in overtime, if priced in play.
Team and closing-lineup FT% plus free-throw rate decide whether intentional-foul sequences end level and drive bonus-heavy OT scoring.

interactions.hypothesis: Tie probability falls steeply in the expected margin, so uncertainty about the margin raises it for mismatches but barely changes it for even games.
Slow, low-three teams have the narrowest margin distributions and the highest tie mass; the two effects compound.
Repeat-tie rates rise or fall across OT periods with foul depletion, so a constant repeat factor misprices the 3+ rung.

Tie probability is a peaked function of the expected margin; averaging it over an uncertain margin raises it for large expected margins (Jensen on the convex tail) and slightly lowers it near zero, so November mismatches carry more OT risk than plug-in estimates suggest.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed OT rate by expected-margin bucket for November versus February games, holding the point estimate fixed.

interactions.hypothesis: Margin sd grows with both possessions and three-point share; tie probability scales roughly with the inverse of sd near even games, so slow, low-three matchups compound into the highest regulation tie rates.
interactions.how_to_test: Two-way table of OT frequency by tempo tercile and combined 3PA-rate tercile among games with expected margin under 3.

interactions.hypothesis: End-game policy only matters in games within one or two possessions in the last minute; a play-for-tie coach increases tie mass only in that regime, so its effect scales with the close-game probability.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress OT occurrence on coach policy index interacted with the pregame probability of a within-3 score at the one-minute mark.

interactions.hypothesis: Once both teams are in the double bonus with starters fouled out, overtime scoring shifts to free throws and the repeat-tie rate changes; the 3+ rung lives almost entirely in this regime.
interactions.how_to_test: Estimate tie-after-OT rate for first versus second and later OT periods and by count of fouled-out starters at period start.

interactions.hypothesis: If the leading team's best free-throw shooters are absent, the fouling strategy of the trailing team becomes more effective, increasing comebacks to a tie in the final minute.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare late-game tie conversions when the leader's top ball handlers' FT% is low versus high, conditioning on margin with 60 seconds left.

interactions.hypothesis: Intentional fouling by the trailing team pays off in proportion to how often it forces free throws times how poorly the leader's shooters convert; a low-FT% closing lineup facing a foul-heavy trailing coach raises both comeback ties and repeat ties in bonus-heavy OTs.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare tie rates in games within 3 points at 60 seconds left, split by the leader's closing-lineup FT% tercile and the trailing coach's intentional-foul rate.

nonlinearities.shape: Gaussian-shaped decay of tie probability in |expected margin|
nonlinearities.why: Tie probability is flat near zero expected margin and falls off rapidly beyond about one margin sd; a linear OT model on spread overstates OT in mismatches and understates it in pick'em games.

nonlinearities.shape: geometric compounding across rungs
nonlinearities.why: Rung N is proportional to the repeat rate raised to N-1, so a relative error of 20 percent in the repeat rate becomes about 44 percent at 3+ and is the main source of rung mispricing.

nonlinearities.shape: inverse square-root scaling of tie mass in possessions
nonlinearities.why: Margin sd grows like the square root of possessions, so tie probability declines concavely as tempo rises; a 10 percent slower game raises tie mass about 5 percent.

mechanism_review.summary: The outcome is a count of consecutive ties. Regulation ends tied with a probability equal to the integer pmf of the final margin at zero: it peaks when the expected margin is near zero, decays roughly like a Gaussian in the expected margin over its sd, and the sd scales with the square root of possessions and with three-point lumpiness. Close finishes are strategic: trailing teams choose to play for the tie or the win, leaders up three foul or defend, and holding for the last shot when level converts ties into overtime or wins. Each five-minute overtime has about one-eighth of regulation possessions (5 of 40 minutes), so its own tie probability is materially higher than regulation's, and player fouls and team-foul bonus carry over and make later periods more free-throw driven. Rung N is P(reg tie) times the product of N-1 repeat-tie probabilities, so higher rungs are tiny and very sensitive to the repeat rate.

stages.name: Expected regulation margin
stages.description: The centre of the regulation margin distribution comes from the fundamentals-only strength gap adjusted for home court, neutral site and confirmed absences. Early in the season (such as November buy games between a mid-major and a Big Ten team) the gap is large on average but uncertain, and that uncertainty must be integrated rather than plugged in, because tie probability is a sharply peaked function of the expected margin.
stages.distribution: Expected margin is approximately normal with a standard error that is largest in November and shrinks with games played and schedule connectivity.

stages.name: Width and lumpiness of the regulation margin
stages.description: Around that centre, the spread of possible final margins scales with expected possessions and with the share of scoring that comes in three-point jumps; slow, interior-oriented matchups produce narrow margin distributions and more ties. Because scores are integers built from 1-, 2- and 3-point events, the probability at exactly zero must come from an integer pmf calibrated on observed overtime frequency, not from a continuous density. The first-rung probability is the P_tie_reg term of the existing overtime-chain input, extended as described in its audit entry.
stages.distribution: Discrete margin pmf with sd roughly 10 to 12 points for a 68-possession game; roughly 6 percent of D1 games reach overtime, so P(margin=0) is above that average for evenly matched teams and falls toward 1 percent or less for 15+ point favourites.

stages.name: Strategic final possessions
stages.description: Games within one or two possessions in the final minute are resolved by choices: trailing by two, go for the tie or the win; trailing by three, take a contested three or a quick two and foul; leading by three, foul to prevent a tying three or defend. Intentional fouling and free-throw shooting move the margin in one- and two-point steps. These choices add or remove mass exactly at zero relative to the smooth model.
stages.distribution: Mixture: most games exit this regime before the final minute; within close finishes, the zero point carries an excess or deficit of order tens of percent relative to smoothed neighbours.

stages.name: Repeat ties in five-minute overtime periods
stages.description: Each overtime has about eight to nine possessions per team (one-eighth of a 68-possession game), so the period margin distribution is narrow and a repeat tie is far more likely than a regulation tie. Player fouls and the second-half team-foul count carry into overtime, so bonus free throws are frequent and starters may foul out; fatigue and depleted rotations make later periods differ from the first. Rung N multiplies the regulation tie by N-1 repeat-tie probabilities.
stages.distribution: Geometric-like chain with period-dependent repeat probability (order 10 to 20 percent per period, to be calibrated), so, with a regulation tie near 6 percent, the unconditional 2+ rung is of order 0.6 to 1.2 percent and 3+ of order 0.06 to 0.25 percent, far higher for tied-late even matchups.

stages.name: Settlement on periods played
stages.description: The ladder counts overtime periods played in the official final result. A short postponement keeps the market alive; cancellation or no start within 48 hours settles at a fair price rather than No, removing void risk from the outcome distribution. How a game halted mid-overtime would count is not stated, and the source of the official result is not named.
stages.distribution: Deterministic mapping from the realised count to nested rungs; void mass sits outside the outcome distribution at an undefined fair price.

talent_strength.note: Strength gap and its uncertainty set the expected regulation margin.

opponent_matchup.note: Matchup enters through combined possessions and combined three-point reliance, which set the width of the margin.

role_personnel.note: Fouled-out players and depleted rotations in overtime periods.

coaching_scheme.note: Play-for-tie versus play-for-win and foul-up-three policies.

environment.note: Home advantage shifts the expected margin.

pace_volume.note: Possessions in regulation and the fixed short OT period.

efficiency_conversion.note: Late free-throw shooting of both teams' closing lineups (FT% and FT rate) moves the margin off or onto zero and sets OT scoring lumpiness.

distribution_variance.note: Integer pmf at zero and the geometric repeat chain.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Whether fatigue in multi-game event weekends or stakes (rivalry, elimination) change repeat-tie rates or end-game risk appetite is unmeasured; no input covers it.

officiating_rules.note: Five-foul limit and team-foul bonus carryover into overtime; rule vintage noted in unresolved.

settlement_contract.note: N+ periods played; 48-hour postponement; fair-price cancellation.

contract_review.settlement_definition: Ladder of nested binaries per game: YES on rung N if at least N overtime periods are played (sample rung 3+, floor_strike 2.5, strike_type greater). Settles on the official final result. If the game is postponed but starts within 48 hours of the original start, the market stays open and settles on the final result; if cancelled or not started within 48 hours, all markets resolve to a fair price. Regulation ties are the only route to rung 1; the rules do not name the stat provider or say how a game suspended during overtime counts.
contract_review.settlement_data_source: 'Official final result' of the game; provider (NCAA, ESPN or Kalshi's data vendor) is not named in the sampled text.
variants_and_edge_cases: Rungs are described as nested (1+, 2+, 3+ ...), but only the 3+ rung (floor_strike 2.5, strike_type greater, so more than 2.5 periods) was sampled; the existence, floor_strike values and wording of the 1+ and 2+ rungs are inferred, not seen (ot_u5).
A game halted during overtime (injury, facility, weather at an outdoor exhibition) and declared final or suspended is not addressed; 'played' periods are not defined for partial periods.
Cancellation or no start within 48 hours settles at a 'fair price', which the rules do not define.
Only one series is sampled; women's or tournament-specific OT series would need separate reading.

tournament_player_milestone.label: Any-player tournament milestone (triple-double, 50-point game)
tournament_player_milestone.target: Whether any player in the whole NCAA men's tournament reaches a single-game stat milestone (triple-double, 50+ points)
tournament_player_milestone.mechanism: The event is a union over every player-game of the tournament (First Four included). Each player-game's chance is a far-tail probability of his stat distribution given minutes, usage, opponent and game script; exposure is the number of games his team survives. A few high-usage scorers or versatile rebound-and-assist players hold most of the mass, so the outcome depends on which teams make the field, how far they advance, star availability, blowout truncation, overtime and the stat source.

inputs.why: Per-game 50+ point probability per candidate, a far-tail quantity.
Per-game probability of 10+ in three of five eligible stats per candidate.
Expected games played per candidate from field entry, survival and availability.
Combines correlated player-games into the any-player probability.
Field and survival simulation that drives exposure and is shared across players.
Field size and play-in games set the total number of team-games.
Usage and per-minute rates are the scale of each player's tails.
Joint covariance of counts decides triple-double probability.
Tournament minutes ceiling for stars multiplies every tail.
A candidate's absence removes his whole contribution.
Tournament opponents are stronger and concede fewer counts by role.
Rebound and assist recording errors matter for 10-count thresholds.
First Four included and the five eligible triple-double categories are set here.
Closing-line-independent competitive-versus-blowout regime mixture of the final margin sets the blowout truncation of star minutes.
Fundamentals-only P(regulation tie) and OT-period chain give the chance of extra minutes for stars in a given matchup.
Coach-specific starter-pull behaviour when ahead converts the blowout regime into actual star minutes.
Matchup possessions scale every count; a fast opponent raises both 50-point and triple-double reach.
Field-level frequency of 50-point games and triple-doubles per tournament by era anchors and bounds the bottom-up union.
A teammate's absence concentrates usage, rebounds and assists on the candidate and lifts his tail probabilities.

interactions.hypothesis: A high-tail scorer on a weak team contributes little because he plays one or two games; exposure and tail multiply.
Star minutes rise in close tournament games and fall in first-round blowouts, so the minutes ceiling depends on matchup closeness.
Triple-double probability is driven by joint, not marginal, counts; independence badly misprices it.
Matchup possessions scale attempt volume, so a fast game raises the 50-point reach more than proportionally.

Each player's contribution to the union is roughly per-game tail probability times expected games; a volume scorer on a likely first-round loser adds little, while a moderate-tail star on a 1 seed adds more through five or six games.
interactions.how_to_test: Decompose the simulated union by player and compare with the product of tail probability and expected games; check against historical 40+ tournament games by seed.

interactions.hypothesis: In close tournament games stars play near 40 minutes; in blowouts they sit early. The regime is set by the matchup's expected margin, so the minutes ceiling and tail probability switch between two levels rather than shifting smoothly.
interactions.how_to_test: Tournament minutes of top-usage players by final-margin bucket versus their regular-season minutes in the same buckets.

interactions.hypothesis: Three counts reaching 10 together depend on shared minutes and pace and on role-specific residual correlation; the minutes draw links all categories, so a high-minutes regime raises triple-double probability more than proportionally.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare observed D1 triple-double frequencies with independent-marginal predictions and with copula predictions by minutes bucket.

interactions.hypothesis: Teammates and opponents share survival paths: if a candidate's team loses early, his games and his teammates' games vanish together, so the union has less effective diversification than independent player-games imply.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare simulated P(YES) under full bracket correlation with an independence approximation using the same marginals.

interactions.hypothesis: Overtime adds about 12 percent more minutes to a full-minute star; because the 50-point event is far in the tail, a modest minutes increase raises its probability by much more than 12 percent.
interactions.how_to_test: Frequency of 40+ point games in OT versus non-OT games for high-usage players, normalised by minutes.

interactions.hypothesis: Possessions scale attempt volume, and the 50-point event sits far in the tail, so a fast matchup raises its probability by more than the possession ratio; a slow game controlled by the opponent pushes the same star far below the 50-point reach.
interactions.how_to_test: Frequency of 35+ point games by matchup expected-possessions tercile for high-usage scorers, normalised by minutes.

nonlinearities.shape: exponential-to-power-law far tail
nonlinearities.why: P(points >= 50) changes by orders of magnitude with small changes in usage and shooting variance; a normal tail assigns essentially zero, a fitted heavy tail does not, so tail shape dominates the estimate.

nonlinearities.shape: concave in per-round win probability through compounding
nonlinearities.why: Expected games equal one plus the cumulative product of round win probabilities, so improving an already strong team adds games at a diminishing rate, while a weak team's exposure is pinned near one.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating union 1 - prod(1 - p_i)
nonlinearities.why: With many small per-game probabilities the union is almost additive, but when a dominant candidate has a large probability the union saturates and other players add less.

mechanism_review.summary: YES occurs if at least one player-game in the tournament crosses the threshold. For each player, the per-game probability is a far-tail quantity: 50 points requires a volume ceiling (about 30 field-goal attempts or many free throws), a hot shooting night and full minutes; a triple-double requires joint 10-counts in three of five stats and is mostly available to versatile guards or forwards (points-rebounds-assists) and elite rim protectors (points-rebounds-blocks). Exposure depends on which teams are in the field, how many games they survive (strong teams play more), and whether the star is healthy. Tournament games change the minutes distribution (shorter rotations in close games, blowouts in lopsided first-round games, occasional overtime) and opponent quality. The union over correlated player-games is concentrated on a few candidates, so tail calibration for them dominates, with settlement sensitive to official stat recording.

stages.name: Field composition and candidate pool
stages.description: Before Selection Sunday the pool of candidate players is uncertain because their teams may not receive bids; afterwards the field (68 teams with First Four, or a different number under a changed format) fixes who can play. Candidates are the small set of high-usage scorers and versatile multi-category producers, plus elite shot-blockers for points-rebounds-blocks triple-doubles.
stages.distribution: Candidate set is concentrated: perhaps 10 to 30 players carry most of the probability, with a long thin tail of others; bid probability is binary per team.

stages.name: Survival and exposure
stages.description: Each team plays until it loses, so expected games per player range from one (play-in losers count) to six or seven for finalists. Survival is shared by teammates, which correlates their chances, and depends on team strength and bracket path. Availability through March (injury, illness) multiplies exposure. During the tournament the same calculation is re-run on the live bracket: only surviving teams' remaining games count, and a recorded milestone ends the question.
stages.distribution: Games per player follow a truncated geometric-like distribution set by round-by-round win probabilities; strong-team stars have high exposure with a long right tail.

stages.name: Per-game minutes and game script
stages.description: Minutes in tournament games differ from the regular season: close elimination games push stars toward 38 to 40 minutes and occasional overtime adds five, while 1-versus-16 style blowouts pull stars early. Foul trouble in physical tournament officiating can cap minutes. Milestones are far-tail events, so these volume shifts have outsized effects.
stages.distribution: Minutes are a mixture of a close-game regime with a high ceiling and a blowout regime truncated at about 25 to 30 minutes; overtime adds a discrete +5 spike.

stages.name: Far-tail stat production
stages.description: Given minutes, a 50-point game requires extreme attempt volume and a hot shooting night against tournament-calibre defences; a triple-double requires correlated high counts in three stats. Per-game probabilities come from compound models with role-pooled tails and joint covariance, adjusted for opponent defence by role and for a possible neutral-site scorekeeper effect on recorded assists and rebounds, whose size is unmeasured (mile_u2).
stages.distribution: Compound overdispersed counts with heavy right tails; per-game 50+ probabilities for even elite scorers are well below 1 percent, triple-double probabilities a few percent at most for top versatile players.

stages.name: Union across player-games and settlement
stages.description: The settled event is the union over all player-games: one minus the probability that none hits. Shared survival paths and shared game scripts correlate player-games. Settlement counts First Four games and five triple-double categories; stat source and corrections are unspecified, and rebound and assist recording at the margin of 10 can decide the outcome.
stages.distribution: Binary and rare: 50-point tournament games and tournament triple-doubles occur in only a minority of tournaments in the modern era, so the prior for 50+ is small and for a triple-double modest; the exact historical counts are to be established by the field-level base-rate input (mile_u5), and the union is dominated by top candidates and sensitive to their tail errors.

officiating_rules.note: Field format and stat recording; tournament officiating crews not modelled separately.

contract_review.settlement_definition: One binary per series per tournament. KXMARMAD3D: YES if any player records a triple-double (10+ in three or more of points, rebounds, assists, blocks, steals) in any game of the men's tournament scheduled Mar 17 to Apr 6, 2026. KXMARMADPTS: YES if any player scores 50+ points in a single game in the same tournament. First Four play-in games count for both. Rules do not name the stat source, do not address stat corrections after the game, and do not say whether overtime statistics count (normally they are part of the game box score).
contract_review.settlement_data_source: Not named in the rules; presumably official NCAA box scores. Source of truth and correction cut-off are unverified.
variants_and_edge_cases: Two thresholds in one archetype: multi-category triple-double (KXMARMAD3D, floor_strike 1, any occurrence) and 50+ points (KXMARMADPTS, floor_strike 50).
Overtime: rules say 'in a game' without excluding overtime, so OT statistics presumably count; not explicitly stated.
Stat corrections by the official scorer after the game (an assist or rebound added or removed) are not addressed and can flip a 9 to a 10.
Tournament window and format are tied to the 2026 dates; a 2027 series under a changed field size would include a different number of games.

Games postponed outside the scheduled window: the wording 'originally scheduled from Mar 17, 2026 to Apr 6, 2026' suggests a postponed tournament game would still count, but the sampled text does not say; a cancelled tournament is not addressed.
